`modelScale` multiplies geometry and placement only, never UV rectangles. The rabbit's scale is far below the rest because it is the only model stood on end — upright it is more than twice as tall as it is long, so the same nets need a much smaller multiplier to stay rabbit-sized. The frog is the one model *shorter* than its hitbox, which is correct: the original's 0.5 cube is generous around a flat animal.

**Only heights come from the reference. Half-widths are ours and are deliberately narrower** — a horse is 0.9 across here against Bedrock's 1.4 — because a wide box catches on doorways and trunks far more than it reads as bulk. Do not "correct" the widths to match a wiki table; the divergence is the design.

Chicken, donkey, rabbit and wolf were moved from Java's heights to Bedrock's on 2026-08-03, so the chicken and rabbit grew, the donkey grew to match the horse (as Bedrock has it), and the wolf shrank slightly. Cow and Bramble stay on their playtested boxes deliberately.

### The smoker

**A furnace that cooks at twice the rate, and it cost no new screen.** `isFurnace` answers true for both families, so the block entity, the screen, opening it, breaking it and spilling its contents all work untouched - none of them ever needed to know which kind it is. Eight ids in the same order as the furnace's, four facings unlit then lit, so the facing is arithmetic rather than a second switch.

**The speed is one multiplier on the whole tick**, not two rates. The reference's smoker cooks in five seconds instead of ten *and* burns its fuel twice as fast, so the items per lump of charcoal are unchanged - running the entire tick at double time reproduces both exactly, and there is no second number to fall out of step.

**Named divergence:** the reference's smoker takes food and nothing else. There is no food yet, so ours cooks whatever a furnace would. Narrowing it is a predicate on the smelt table the day food exists.

### The smithing table

**Two inputs and a result**, borrowing the furnace's slot regions so the whole click, drag and shift-click path works unchanged. The result is a **preview** computed from what is in front of it, like a crafting grid, rather than something the block is slowly making - so it goes through the crafting take path, with `pendingResult` and `spendIngredients` standing in for the two calls that used to be hard-coded to the grid matcher.

**It is where the Emberite upgrade lives**, and that is the point of building it: the upgrade shipped as a shapeless two-item recipe for exactly one milestone, which was a named divergence made because there was no table. `smithingResult(base, addition)` is its own small table rather than a `Recipe`, because an upgrade *keeps* the item it is given and no grid pattern can express that. The reference also needs a template item, which we have no source for.

**No facing ids.** The reference keeps a smithing table's faces pointing the same way however it is placed, so which side you see is a fact about the block - the crafting table's arrangement exactly.

### The chest, and the four families that are one

**`isChest` covers six families: the plain chest, the barrel, the trapped chest, the ender chest, all seventeen stowboxes and the twelve loot chests.** One screen, one block entity, one spill on break, one shift-click rule. That single predicate is the whole cost of five of them, and it is the pattern to reach for whenever a new container arrives — the loot chests cost nothing beyond the predicate and one exclusion in `chestPairs`.

> ⛔ **Widening it is also what kills the early-outs already sitting behind it.** `dropForBlock` had `if (isChest) return Chest`, so a barrel dropped a plain chest; the placement path handed every chest to `chestFacing`, so a trapped chest became a plain one the moment it was set down. **Grep every user before widening a family test.**

**Twenty-seven slots, and the first screen with a slot region of its own.** The furnace and the smithing table both borrow `craftSlots`' first two. A chest cannot: its contents are neither ingredients nor a result, they outlive the screen being closed, and there are twenty-seven of them against a maximum grid of nine. So it gets `Region::Chest`, and `stackAt` resolves that straight into the block's own storage. **The hopper borrows that same region** for its five, which is why it needed no click, drag or shift-click code of its own.

**Two exceptions are carved out of the family deliberately.** The **ender chest** resolves to twenty-seven slots the *player* owns rather than the block's, checked before the block map is consulted at all — so every ender chest in the world is the same window. The **stowbox** is the one container whose contents do not fall out when it is broken; see its own section below.

**Closing is where the shared buffer bites.** A crafting grid's contents are handed back to the player, because they exist only while the screen is up. A furnace's are **discarded** — they were only a view onto the block, which keeps its own copy. For one milestone the furnace branch did neither: it skipped the give-back (right) but did not clear the slots (wrong), so the copies were still sitting there when the next screen opened, showed up in its crafting grid, and were handed over when *that* closed. Two keystrokes for free items. A chest needs nothing here, because its stacks were never in the buffer at all.

**Shift-click crosses the two halves rather than shuffling within one.** In every other screen a shift-click moves between hotbar and storage. With a container open the interesting move is inventory→container and container→inventory, so `quickMoveTargets` takes an earlier branch gated on `isContainer(kind)` and returns the *other* store. It offers **only the slots that screen shows**, or shift-clicking into a hopper would put items in the twenty-two slots of the shared struct that nothing can reach.

**Persistence mirrors the furnace exactly** — `chests.dat` beside `furnaces.dat`, same magic-version-seed header, same atomic temp-then-rename, same rule that an empty table *deletes* the file rather than leaving a stale one that would restore chests the player has already broken. `PlacedChest` is written as raw bytes and has the same `static_assert` guarding that.

**Four facing ids**, unlike the smithing table, because the latch is on one face. `chestFacing` has the same two overloads the furnace's does, and the trapped chest and ender chest keep **their own** accessors rather than sharing one — a defaulted family parameter is exactly how a trapped chest turns into a plain one.

**Two chests shoulder to shoulder open as one fifty-four slot container**, and the pairing is **worked out from position alone, never remembered**. That is the important decision: a saved "who is joined to whom" would have to survive a reload, stay consistent when a neighbour is broken, and be written into `chests.dat`. Instead `chestPartnerAt` walks back to the start of the run of matching chests and pairs off in twos from there, so both halves always agree and the answer costs no saved state. A run of three leaves the third single; a run of four is two pairs. They must share a facing, and they join **across** the latch (`chestJoinsAlongX`) so the side faces touch, never front to back.

> **`chestPairs(id)` is what stops the walk joining things that must never join.** Its only test is "the neighbour is the same id", so without an explicit exclusion two barrels, two ender chests or two stowboxes standing side by side would silently become one fifty-four slot container.

The two blocks stay two separate `Chest` entries holding twenty-seven each - only the screen joins them, so breaking one half spills only that half and leaves the other as an ordinary chest.

**The double chest is the first screen taller than the standard card.** `panelPixelHeight(kind)` and `storageShiftY(kind)` replaced two constants; `kPixel` stays fixed to the 166-tall panel on purpose, so a taller screen grows downward at the same slot size rather than shrinking everything to fit. The panel art is the ordinary one with its empty middle **stretched** by three rows and the player's grid moved down with it, so no frame or bevel is redrawn.

**A double chest is textured as one wide chest**, so the latch sits in the middle of a single long lid rather than appearing twice. This cost **six** layers rather than the eight ids once predicted, because the half is not stored in the block at all — it is *derived*. `chestHalfFor(facing, dx, dz)` turns "which way am I facing and which neighbour am I joined to" into `Left` or `Right`, `gatherVolume` packs that answer into two spare bits of the flags array the waterlogged bit already occupies, and the mesher passes it to `blockTextureLayer`. **Zero extra block ids and zero extra memory**, and nothing new to save — the half is recomputed from position exactly the way the pairing itself is.

The outer side face was measured against the single chest's and is **pixel-identical** (0 differing texels), so it is reused rather than duplicated; only the top, front and back differ per half. The back needs the opposite alignment from the front, because a back face's `u` runs the other way in the mesher's face table.

> ⚠️ **The paired lids are not mirrored, and that was measured.** They used to be, on the theory that a box's UP rect unwraps with `u` reversed — which a single chest can never contradict, because its lid is symmetric. Per-column luminance settles it: the dark border sits at column 0 of `normal_right`'s UP rect and column 14 of `normal_left`'s, exactly where each front's does. Mirrored, both borders land against the seam and every double chest wears a dark line down the middle of its lid.

> ⚠️ **Mojang's `normal_left.png` is the viewer's *right* half, and `normal_right.png` is the viewer's *left*.** The names describe the chest's own handedness, not the camera's. This was settled by measurement, not by reading the filename: per-column luminance shows `normal` carries a border at *both* ends while each half carries one at a single end, and the buried face is the transparent one. Trusting the filename puts the latch on the outside corners and splits the lid down the middle.

**Named divergences:** no opening animation, no moving lid, and the block is a full opaque cube rather than the reference's slightly-inset model.

### The stowbox

**Our name for the shulker box**, since *Shulker* is Mojang's coinage. Seventeen of them, plain and sixteen dyes, and they are the one container whose contents **do not fall out when it is broken** — they move onto the item, which is the entire point of the thing.

**The contents ride in `ItemStack::damage`.** That is the trick, and it is why this cost no save-format bump anywhere: `damage` is already a per-stack number, already written into `player.dat`, already stored in `chests.dat`, and now carried by a dropped entity too. For a tool it is wear; for a stowbox it is a handle into a side table. Nothing else had to learn a new field.

- Breaking one allocates a handle, moves the block's `Chest` into `stowed`, and spawns the drop carrying that handle.
- Placing one looks the handle up, installs the contents on the block, and **frees the handle**, so nothing accumulates across a session.
- `stowboxes.dat` (magic `VXSB`, version 1) saves the table. It is a new file rather than a changed one, so an absent file is simply an empty table and there is nothing to migrate.

> ⚠️ **A stowbox must never stack, and a `static_assert` holds it.** Two merging would silently pick one handle and lose the other's contents outright. That is the same reason a tool does not stack, and `maxStackFor` states both rules in one place.

**`ItemEntities::spawn` and `Inventory::add` both gained a `damage` parameter** to carry it, and that fixed a pre-existing bug on the way: a damaged tool spilled out of a broken chest used to come back undamaged. **`dropStack` now takes the whole stack** at every one of those sites, because a parameter that can be omitted is a field that will be — see "Items and drops", and `slots::roomFor` for the merging half of the same rule.

### The hopper

**Five slots, one row, and it borrows `Region::Chest` outright** — so the entire container path, clicking, shift-clicking, saving and spilling on break, already covered it. It stores its five in the same twenty-seven-slot `Chest` struct and simply never touches the rest; `containerSlots(id)` is the one place that difference lives, and reading past it would let a hopper hold items no screen can reach.

**One item every eight ticks**, the reference's own rate. Each pass pushes out of the spout first and then pulls from whatever is above, so a chain carries an item one step per hopper per tick rather than all the way along in whichever order the map happened to be in.

> ⚠️ **Positions are gathered before anything moves.** Pushing into a container nobody has opened yet *creates* its block entity, and creating one while walking the map is exactly the rehash that invalidates the walk.

**Five states, not six.** A spout points down or at any of the four sides and never up; `hopperWithSideSpout` folds anything that is not a compass direction to the plain downward one, which is what makes a hopper placed on a floor behave.

### The stonecutter

**One block in, and the cuts it offers laid out beside it.** The results are previews like a smithing table's, so they use `Region::CraftResult` — but there are three of them, and it is the only screen where that region's index means anything. `resultSlotCount(kind)` is what says so, and `build()` takes an array of results rather than one.

**Which cuts a block has is a reverse lookup over the family tables, not a table of its own.** `stonecutterOption(parent, n)` scans `kStairFamilies`, `kSlabFamilies` and `kWallFamilies` for the family naming that block as its parent. A second list could only fall out of step with the first — a new stair material would silently offer nothing here. Yields are the reference's: two slabs, one of everything else.

### The bell, the cauldron and the lectern

**The bell rings and that is all of it.** The reference's swing is an animated model rather than a block state, and there are no animated block models here, so the sound is the whole behaviour. It cost one new `SoundEvent` — the count is 162 now.

**The cauldron holds nought to six**, which is the reference's own range rather than a third of it. A bucket fills or empties it outright; a glass bottle takes two of the six, which is the arithmetic behind "a cauldron holds three bottles". How full it is does not survive being broken.

**The lectern holds one book**, and it borrows the chest map's first slot rather than owning a map of its own — so it saves, spills on break and survives a reload with no new machinery at all.

> ⛔ **Six workstations were full opaque cubes until 2026-08-10** — the bell, the cauldron, the composter, the grindstone, the stonecutter and the brewing stand — which meant each of them culled its neighbours' faces and showed a hole through the world for a couple of blocks around. They are `Model` blocks now, built from the reference's own JSON geometry: stone posts and a plank bar round a gold bell, a log-legged wheel, a bench with a saw plate, a rod in three base plates with three blades, and two hollow tubs with a contents plate inside.

**Two texture layers were appended after every existing run, and both are appended for the same reason: a face that is not one of the block's own six.** `stonecutter_saw.png` is a plane standing out of the bench, named by `kStonecutterSawSprite`; `bed_head_north.png` is the end of a bed's head, named by `kBedHeadNorthSprite` and shared by all sixteen colours because the reference shares it too. A third followed on 2026-08-10 — `composter_compost.png`, `kComposterCompostSprite` — because the tub's own top texture is a rim with a transparent middle and the contents plate samples exactly that middle, so compost drew nothing at every level below eight. Appending is the rule here — anything inserted in the middle silently slides every layer behind it and mistextures them all.

> ⛔ **Twenty blocks were full opaque cubes painted from art with real holes in it, and both halves of that had to be fixed.** Being opaque, each culled its neighbours' faces; not being a cutout, its empty texels drew as black. Marking them cutout alone made it worse — the holes became **gaps**, because the art is transparent where the *model* is smaller. So the ten that are genuinely not cubes now have real geometry from the reference's own JSON: the **anvil** (a plinth, two waists and an overhanging top), the **end portal frame** (13/16), the **enchanting table** (12/16), the **sculk sensor** (8/16), the **sculk shrieker** (a base and a narrower drum), the **campfire** (four logs), **scaffolding** (four corner posts under a deck) and the **hopper** (a rim, four walls, a funnel and a spout). The **copper grates** and the **spawner** really are `cube_all` and stayed cubes. Collision and the targeting outline take the whole silhouette as one box rather than every plinth.

### The id space

`BlockId` is a **`std::uint16_t`**, and `ItemId::kFirstToolItem` is **4096**. Both were widened together when the byte-wide id space ran down to three free values.

**Why widening rather than reclaiming.** The eight water levels and eight stair orientations are the two biggest consumers of ids, and packing them into a side array would have bought back roughly thirty values — a year's worth at the rate blocks are being added, in exchange for unpicking `isWater`, `waterLevel` and `blockShape`, a second per-cell array to save and load, and the same conversation again later. Widening costs one byte per cell **once** and ends the question permanently.

> **3,309 of the 4,096 are used at the last probe, and `Mining.hpp` caps a compiling tree at 3,584** (`kBlockIdCount`). ⚠️ **Corrected three times on 2026-08-19 and the last correction is the instructive one.** *Was "3,269 … (2026-08-18)"; then "≥ 3,339" at 10:09, which is **impossible in a tree that compiles**; then "[3,073 … 3,328]" at 10:20, which was true for three minutes.* The last probe-measured value is **3,309** (compile-time `Show<N>` probe, ~06:00). The 10:09 version added a 24-id `BeeNestRunFirst..Last` (`kBeehiveHoneyLevels * 4`) and a 6-id `FarmlandMoistureRunFirst..Last` (`kFarmlandMoistureLevels − 2` — eight *states* are six new *ids*, because levels 0 and 7 already had them) to reach 3,339; **both run sizes are right and the sum is still wrong**, because it assumed the probe predated both runs and nothing was checked that could say so. **`game/src/item/Mining.hpp` bounds it without a build:** `kMiningRows` is assembled from 256-id chunks, and a `static_assert` compares the chunks the enum *needs* against the chunks actually *written*. That cap was **3,328** over thirteen hand-written pointers until **10:23:32**, when the constant was split into `kMiningChunkCount` (derived need) and `kMiningChunkCapacity` (written supply, now 14), lifting the cap to **3,584** and the headroom from ~19 ids to ~275. A second `static_assert` pins the capacity against the last pointer in the list, so raising one number alone cannot silence it — bug shape #11. **What would make this false:** a re-probe, another chunk landing, or a run appended after 10:25:01 today (`Block.hpp`'s mtime as this was written). That is four fifths of the id ceiling, and the run rate is no longer slow — doors alone took 384, beds 128, the loot-chest run took **44 for eleven tables**, and a single bee nest cost 24. **A family that would spend hundreds of ids on orientation deserves a moment's thought about a side array first.**

**The 4096 ceiling is not the type's limit, it is the item space's.** Block items share the block numbering and non-block items start above them, so the two runs must not collide. A `static_assert` on `kLastBlock` holds the line, and it is the thing that will fail loudly if blocks ever do get that far.

**Old inventories still read correctly** because `upgradeLegacyItemId` shifts any stored id at or above the old 256 boundary up by the difference. Chest and furnace files carry their own version constants, so the shift is applied exactly once, only to files written before the move.

**What it costs, measured.** A chunk's block array went 32 KB → 64 KB, so a resident chunk is 36 KB → 68 KB including its waterlogged bits. At `render_distance=8` with 1083 chunks resident the process peaks at **328 MB** working set, of which the widen accounts for about **34 MB**. For scale, the reference eats roughly 1.6 GB at a comparable render distance. Growth here is expected and is answered by optimisation over time — a palette per chunk would give most of it back whenever that becomes worth doing.

### Adding a block type

Eleven steps, and the compiler catches almost none of them. Work through the list.

**First, check whether it is a *cut shape* of a block that already exists** — a stair, a slab, a wall, a fence, a gate, a carpet or a pane. If it is, none of this applies: add one row to the matching `kXFamilies` table in `Block.hpp`, bump the count beside the enum, and add the recipe loop's material. Everything else is forwarded through `shapedParent`. That is how six hundred and forty blocks arrived with no art and no table rows.

1. Append a `BlockId`. **Never insert** — ids are written to disk, so moving one rewrites every saved chunk. There is plenty of room: `BlockId` is a `std::uint16_t` and a `static_assert` holds the last id below 4096.

   **The table-driven run is now seven runs, and that is why.** Each run is followed in the enum by something that is not a table block — the hive, the cut-shape runs, the doors, the beds — so growing any of them in place would renumber everything above it and silently rewrite saved worlds. Each new run is appended at the end instead, and `isExtraBlock` spans all seven exactly as `isCrossBlock` already spans its two. `extraBlockIndex` maps all seven onto one **580-row** table; **their sprite layers stay in one run**, because `ExtraBlockInfo::layer` is an offset from `kTableSpritesFirst` and one origin is easier to keep true than seven.
2. Move `kLastBlock` to the new id. Anything that walks every block reads it, so a stale one silently leaves the newest block out of the catalogue.
3. Map its texture to `block\<name>` in `tools/make-reference-blocks.ps1` and re-run it. Our own 16×16 in `assets/textures/blocks/` is the fallback; a missing file falls back to the white layer and is named in the log.

   **`kTableSprites` is derived, not written down.** It was the single most dangerous constant in the file — nothing asserted it, and one too small meant the last few blocks silently sampled whichever run followed, which is a wrong texture with no error anywhere. `maxTableLayer()` now scans the table for the highest `.layer`/`.topLayer` and adds one.
4. Add its filename to the texture list in `game/src/Main.cpp`, in layer order.
5. Add an entry to `TextureLayer` in `game/src/world/Block.hpp` — **and move `SpawnEggFirst` by however many you added** (it is 67 today). Getting this wrong does not fail; it slides all thirty-six sprites of the *first* spawn egg run *and* the eleven resource sprites behind them. `Main.cpp` compares it against the loaded list at startup and names the mismatch.

   **Spawn eggs live in two runs and that is deliberate.** The first is 36 long and is followed on disk by the resources, the buckets and the water frames; species 36 and up take a *second* run at the very end (`kExtraSpawnEggFirst` / `ItemId::SpawnEggExtraFirst`). Widening the first would shift every resource and bucket id, and an item id is written into the player's saved inventory. `spawnEggIndex`, `spawnEggForIndex` and `itemTextureLayer` all span both runs; **`allItems()` re-orders them so the catalogue shows all fifty-six together** even though their ids are not contiguous.
6. Return it from `blockTextureLayer()`.
7. Name it in `blockName()`.

   > ⭐ **`blockName` is proven total at compile time and can no longer fall to `default: return "Air"`.** `everyBlockNamed(stride)` walks every id in the space and asserts that nothing but `BlockId::Air` answers "Air"; seven `static_assert`s run it at seven strides, and an eighth holds that the seven strides cover the whole id count. Both sides are `constexpr`, so it cannot rot — a block added without a name fails the build instead of appearing in the catalogue as air. Nobody could say statically how many ids were reaching that catch-all before this, across forty-odd family predicates and 2,223 ids.
8. Give it a category in `categoryFor()` in `item/Item.hpp`, or it silently lands in the Items tab. **If it spends ids on orientation or contents, add its family test to `isCanonicalBlockItem` too** — otherwise the catalogue shows one row per id. The beehive's eight appeared as eight separate entries until it was named there, and the user found it by opening the inventory.
9. Give it hardness, a harvest tool and a tier in `item/Mining.hpp`, and a blast resistance in `world/Explosion.cpp`. **Only the blast resistance has a default now.**

   > ⭐ **A block with no mining answer is a build error, not a bland one.** `kMiningRows` is sized by `kBlockIdCount` and filled by walking the enum, so an appended run cannot fall outside a range test the way it could when four hand-written accessors each carried their own — but sizing alone only guarantees a row *exists*. The final `default:` therefore returns a sentinel that cannot be self-consistent, and the fifth sweep invariant fails the build naming the id. Add the run to `derivedHardness`, `derivedTool` and `derivedTier` and the sentinel goes away.
   >
   > This is what closed the biggest per-block hole in the file. Runs 1, 3, 4 and 7 had no `harvestTier` branch at all, so the iron, gold, diamond, emerald, lapis and copper blocks, tuff, calcite, amethyst, deepslate bricks and the prismarines all fell to the hand tier and dropped themselves to a fist — and **every stair, slab and wall cut from them inherited it through `shapedParent`**. 291 ids changed harvest requirement and 100 stopped defaulting to hardness 1.0. `blastResistance` still has the sixth run written **twice**, byte for byte, which costs nothing and is the same shape: a table whose runs are copied rather than derived.

   > **Anything that is not simply "one of itself" needs a row in `item/BlockDrops.hpp` as well** — a different item, a count range, a chance, or an alternative. Blocks that drop themselves need nothing there; `dropsForBlock` asks `dropForBlock` for the identity of the 96.6% that do.
10. If it is not a full cube, add it to `blockShape()`, and to `isCutout()` if it has transparent pixels. **A new `BlockShape` needs nothing in the mesher's two lists** — `usesShapePass` owns that question now — but it does need a `collisionBoxes` case, and a `selectionBoxes` one if it collides with nothing.
11. **If it has a front, add it to `blockFacing()`** — that is what the *icon* reads. The world mesher passes a real direction, so a miss there renders correctly in the world and wrongly in every inventory and hotbar slot: both visible side faces get `Unknown`, which `blockTextureLayer` answers with the front. The furnace, the chest and the smithing table have each hit this.

Blocks whose faces differ are handled by the `BlockFace` parameter rather than by special cases in the mesher. Grass is the worked example: top, bottom and sides all resolve to different layers. Sandstone and the bookshelf are the newer ones.

### The four box sets, and which one is the drawn shape

A block has **four** different box answers and they are all deliberately different from each other. Picking the wrong one is the recurring bug in this area, so they are named here together:

| | What it is | Who asks |
|---|---|---|
| `collisionBoxes` | What you bump into | Physics, the player, creatures |
| `selectionBoxes` | What the crosshair picks | Raycast, the outline |
| `modelSilhouette` / `postBoxes` | **One box, the union** | Redstone collision, wall torches |
| **`drawnBoxes`** | **Exactly what the mesher emitted** | The mesher, and anything drawing *onto* a block |

A fence's drawn rails are not the posts you walk into; a plant's pick column is not its two blades; a lantern is silhouetted as one box and drawn as four. **`drawnBoxes(id, connections, opaqueAbove)` is the single owner of the last row and the mesher itself calls it**, so a second copy cannot drift. The two facts an id cannot carry are passed in: what a fence reaches toward (`connectionBits`) and whether a vine has a ceiling. `worldDrawnBoxes` in `Collision.hpp` supplies both from the world, beside its two twins.

> ⛔ **A `Cross` plant has no box answer at all** — it is two crossed quads, and `drawnBoxes` returns nothing for it. A caller that forgets draws a cage round every flower. There is a `static_assert` on exactly that, and it was proved to fire before being trusted.

### Breaking cracks

Ten `destroy_stage_*` layers appended at the **very end** of the sprite run (`kDestroyStageFirst`), drawn over whatever is being mined. `destroyStageLayer(progress)` picks one and clamps both ends.

- **The geometry is `worldDrawnBoxes`**, which is the whole reason that function exists: cracks on a torch, a fence or a slab have to sit on the shape that is actually there, not on a cube round it. `Cross` plants get the mesher's own two blades.
- **It needed no new pipeline, no blending and no depth change**, and that is a measured fact rather than a hope: each stage is 16×16 with the crack lines at **alpha 255** and the field between them at **alpha 1**, so it is already a cutout. Drawn through the ordinary lit path, the alpha test throws the field away and only the lines survive — which is also why they cannot stamp depth across the face.
- **Staging must not flatten them.** They are named beside water and the glass in `make-reference-blocks.ps1`; the shape test reads them as translucent block art and would turn every stage into an opaque grey tile that paints the block solid while you mine.
- Vertex colour is full white so a crack reads in a cave, and the mesh is **world space with no transform**, rebuilt only when the stage or the block changes — ten times per block at most. It is torn down the frame digging stops.
- **They replaced the HUD progress bar rather than joining it.** A bar under the crosshair and cracks on the block are the same fact told twice, and the cracks are the one that tells you *which* block. Removed at the user's word: _"remove the progress bar for breaking a block, whole point of cracks is that."_ `breakProgress` still exists — it is what `destroyStageLayer` reads.
- **The darkness is randomised from grey to black, smoothly.** The two light channels stay at full and the **face shade** carries it, because `diffuseLevel` multiplies that straight into the result — it is the one honest per-vertex darkness knob the lit path offers, and being per-vertex is what makes the shade drift *along* a crack rather than jump. One `value3D` sample at each corner's own world position, so two quads meeting on an edge take the same sample and the darkness carries across the join.

> ⛔ **One octave, and a measured contrast stretch.** Octaves sum toward their mean, so an fbm here would have spent almost all its time in the middle and every crack would have been the same grey — the distribution trap this project has now been caught by five times. Even one octave is a bell: **measured over 72000 samples, 42% landed in the middle fifth**. Widening about the centre by `kCrackContrast = 1.5` gives 8% in each end decile against 15% in the middle; 2.5 was tried and pins nearly two cracks in five to an extreme, which reads as two colours rather than a range.

Appearing in the **world** is separate from existing: that is a row in the biome table, a few lines in `TerrainGenerator.cpp`'s ground-cover pass, or a row in its ore table.

> ⛔ **A block that exists but is placed nowhere is invisible, and nothing warns you.** Thirteen plants and both mushrooms were added over two milestones and generated *nowhere at all*, because the ground-cover pass held one hardcoded eight-entry flower array and nothing else. The catalogue showed them, the textures loaded, the build was clean. **After adding anything natural, confirm it against a census** — and see the box below about which biomes a census actually covers.

### What the ground-cover pass places

One pass over each surface column, in `TerrainGenerator.cpp`. Eleven things now, all verified generating by count:

| What | Where | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| Grass, fern | any grassy top | fern only in `Forest`-tagged biomes, 35% of the cover there |
| 12 flowers | grassy top | **regional** — a cell hash picks one species per 64-block region, with 30% strays so a region is not a monoculture |
| Blue orchid | `Swamp` | overrides the regional pick entirely; it is the swamp's alone |
| Cactus, dead bush | `Dry` + sand, clear of the shore | cactus 1%, 1–3 tall |
| Sweet berry bush | `Cold` | 0.6% |
| Brown / red mushroom | `Wet` | 0.6% |
| Bamboo | `Wet` **and** `Forest` | 4.5%, 3–7 tall |
| Sugar cane | surface exactly one above sea level | 18%, 2–3 tall — the waterline strip a river or lake edge produces |
| Lily pad | `Swamp` or `River`, unfrozen, shallow | 5%, placed **at** sea level on the water surface |
| Coral, sea pickle | warm ocean bed | pickles only on a reef |
| Kelp, seagrass | any ocean bed | |

> ⚠️ **The worldgen probe's block census covers about 352×352 blocks around the origin and contained only five biomes** — river, jagged peaks, meadow, windswept hills and plains. The biome *share* list is sampled far more coarsely over a much wider area, so it lists biomes the census cannot see. **A zero in the census is not evidence a plant is broken** if the plant's biome is not in that list; it took a temporary wide scan across ±70 chunks to show that ferns, cactus, bamboo, berries and mushrooms had been working all along.

A multi-block plant grows with a helper that **stops at the top of the chunk** rather than writing into the one above. A stalk near a chunk ceiling is simply shorter there — writing across the boundary would break generation purity, which is the rule that lets chunks be generated in any order on any thread.

> ⛔ **A plant standing at `plantY == 0` is a real placement, not an out-of-range case.** That is the column whose surface is the last block of the chunk *below*: the plant belongs to this chunk and the ground it stands on does not. Refusing it deleted every plant at y 32 and y 64 — two bare horizontal bands through every world, at each chunk boundary. The ground is now asked the pure way, `surfaceCarvedAt`, which is exactly the `plantY - 1` question (has a cave taken the top block) with no neighbour read. **This is what `kChunkFormatVersion` 5 is for**: it changes what generation produces, so a chunk saved before it would sit beside a regenerated neighbour that disagrees.

### Authoring

`tools/make-block-textures.ps1` generates the current set. The rules it follows, taken from real block-texture reference:

- **No interpolation, blending or gradients.** Every pixel is one palette entry chosen outright. Smooth noise reads as melted blobs even after quantization, and looks uncanny.
- **Tight value ranges.** Stone spans only a few near greys. Wide contrast makes terrain look like static.
- **Weighted palette selection**, so most pixels land on middle tones and extremes stay sparse.
- **Short horizontal runs**, never large patches.
- **Accent pixels**, such as the grey pebbles in soil, which are what stop brown reading as a blanket.
- **Direction beats noise where the material has a grain.** Bark is per-column stripes with occasional vertical breaks, not isotropic noise stretched vertically. Log end grain is **square** rings (Chebyshev distance), not circular ones — concentric squares are what reads as a cut log at 16×16.
- **Leaves are baked green.** Reference art stores them greyscale because the original tints them per biome at runtime; we have no tinting stage, so the colour goes into the texture.

The PNGs are ordinary files and may be edited by hand instead; the script is a starting point, not a pipeline step. `tools/preview-textures.ps1` magnifies textures into a labelled sheet, because 16×16 cannot be judged at actual size.

Third-party textures kept for visual reference live in `reference/`, which is gitignored and deliberately outside `assets/` so the build cannot copy them into the game.

### Items and drops

**`ItemId` is a separate type from `BlockId`.** Every placeable block has an item form, but not every item is a block — a tool never is. Block items share the block's numbering so there is only one list to maintain, and non-block items start at `kFirstToolItem`, which is **4096**.

`dropForBlock` decides what breaking yields **in identity**. It is a table, not an identity function: stone gives cobblestone, grass gives dirt, an ore gives its resource, and all eight stair orientations collapse to one item so an inventory cannot fill with rotations of the same thing.

> ⛔ **It is no longer the whole answer, and `game/src/item/BlockDrops.hpp` is.** A single `ItemId` and a fixed count could not say "gravel gives flint *instead of* gravel", and could not say "oak leaves roll a sapling, a stick and an apple, each on its own chance". `BlockDrop` carries up to **three** `DropEntry{item, min, max, salt, chanceNum, chanceDen}` rows — three because oak leaves are the Overworld's worst case — and it is a value rather than an allocation, because it is returned on every break. **The old pair is still correct for the identity of 96.6% of ids and is still what answers them**, so the 640 cut shapes, the candles, both door halves and every container state stay in the one place a family rule already lives.

**A count is a range now, not a midpoint.** `dropCountForBlock` flattened the reference's ranges to fixed numbers — copper 3, redstone 4, lapis 6 — and **142 block ids had a wrong drop between them: 108 wrong in identity and 34 wrong in count**. Copper is 2–5, redstone 4–5, lapis 4–9, melon 3–7, glowstone 2–4, carrots and potatoes 2–5. Two duplication exploits closed at the same time: **the monster spawner and budding amethyst dropped themselves**, which is an infinite spawner and an infinite geode.

> ⭐ **`dropStack` is the single owner of putting a stack on the floor**, and `kDropPickupDelay` is the single owner of how long before it can be picked up again. Every site that spills something — a broken block, a broken container, a blast, a creature's loot, a click that has nowhere to put what the cursor holds — goes through it, so none of them can forget to carry `damage`, to give the stack an outward velocity, or to arm the delay. A second copy of that delay is a second thing to get wrong, which is why it is named rather than typed at each call.

> ⛔ **Salt semantics, and gravel is the whole reason the field exists.** **Entries sharing a salt are mutually exclusive alternatives settled by one roll**, in table order by cumulative weight; **entries with different salts are independent rolls.** Gravel gives gravel *or* flint, so its two entries share salt 0. Written as two independent rolls at 10% and 90% they would both fire about one time in eleven, which is a duplication bug wearing the costume of a drop table. Leaves use salts 0, 1 and 2 and genuinely are three separate questions.

**A roll is derived from the block's own position**, never from a running generator, so breaking the same gravel twice gives the same haul and a reloaded save does not re-roll it. `dropHash(x, y, z, salt, nonce)` is the single owner. **The exception is anything renewable** — crops, stems, leaves, melon, pumpkin and the mushroom blocks — which mixes in a session-local break nonce through `rerollsEachBreak`, because a deterministic position is a *farm-able constant* for anything that regrows: a known "apple cell" was an infinite apple at 100%. A `static_assert` holds both halves, that no nonce reaches a one-shot block and that a nonce genuinely changes a melon.

**What the player brought is a `BreakContext`**, not four arguments, so Silk Touch and Fortune can arrive later without touching a call site — neither exists here, and both default to "no". `explosion` is Bedrock's blast rule in one flag: a blast drops as if mined with an unenchanted diamond tool, or an empty hand where shears would be wanted. **A default-constructed context is bare hands and means it** — a cauldron, an ender chest and a cobweb all yield nothing to one, so every call site must pass what is actually held. **The tier gate is still `yieldsDrop`'s**, not this table's; what lives here is the narrower question a tier cannot answer, which is what tool changes *what* falls.

**Eleven resource items** — coal, raw iron/gold/copper, their three ingots, diamond, emerald, lapis and redstone — sit **after** the whole spawn egg run, so adding one can never shift an egg's layer. `kResourceItems` and a `static_assert` tie the count to the run's own endpoints.

**A bucket carries water**, and it is appended after the resource run for the same reason that run sits after the eggs — an item id is written into the saved inventory, so anything inserted earlier makes an old world come back holding the wrong things. `ItemId::kLastItem` is now the single owner of where the run ends, the way `kLastBlock` is for blocks, and `allItems()` reads it.

Filling it needs its own ray. Water has no selection geometry, so the ordinary aim passes straight through to the riverbed — `raycast` therefore takes a `stopAtWater` flag rather than gaining a second walker beside it, which is the same "one walker, two questions" arrangement `hasLineOfSight` already uses. It fills from a **source** only, because scooping a flowing cell leaves a gap its own source refills a moment later and reads as the bucket having done nothing; and it places `Water0`, a source rather than a full level, because a flowing level drains itself on the next fluid update. An empty bucket stacks to sixteen and a full one not at all, both the reference's. Swapping full for empty is the **cost** of using it, which is the one thing creative is allowed to skip.

**Ores demand the reference's own tier.** Gold, redstone, diamond and emerald need an iron pickaxe, obsidian and ancient debris a diamond one. They all sat at stone until 2026-08-06 for one reason - stone was the highest tier that existed - and that was a named divergence rather than a balance decision. It is closed.

**Dropped items are the smallest possible entity** — position, velocity, stack — and resolve on all three axes through `overlapsSolid` and `highestSurfaceBelow`, the same helpers the player and the creatures use. They were vertical-only until 2026-08-05, on the reasoning that a drop is small and decorative; the cost was that **nothing stopped one entering a block sideways, and once inside, the ground probe found that block and lifted the drop onto its top** — so an item nudged against a step climbed it. Their geometry is **rebuilt every frame rather than transformed**, because world meshes are drawn with an identity model matrix and the shader recovers normals from screen-space derivatives of world position; that only holds while vertex positions *are* world positions. The mesh handle is reused, or every frame would retire a GPU buffer.

**A drop gets the same three guards everything else that moves already had**, added 2026-08-17 and each of them a rule that existed elsewhere and had not travelled here: the frame step is clamped to `kMaxDeltaSeconds` (0.05) exactly as the player's and the creatures' are, the column is asked `columnResident` before anything is simulated — an absent chunk reads as air, so a drop over the streaming frontier falls out of the world and is buried when the chunk arrives — and the fall is **swept in slices of at most `kMaxSweepStep`** rather than resolved at the destination, since a floor thinner than the step falls between two samples. Two `static_assert`s hold the pair together: slices must overlap the drop's own size, and a clamped frame at terminal velocity must not need more slices than intended.

> ⛔ **`dropStack` is the single owner of "a whole `ItemStack` leaves the player and lands in the world".** Eleven paths built a drop out of an item and a count and left `damage` behind — the death drop, the Q-drop, the throw, both halves of a chest, a furnace's spill, an explosion's spill, the screen give-back and the shift-click craft loop. `damage` is a tool's wear **and** it is which stored contents a stowbox holds, so every one of those quietly repaired the tool and emptied the box. It takes the stack, so the field cannot be forgotten by omission; `ItemEntities::spawn` still takes the pieces for the few callers that genuinely have only pieces.

**A non-block drop is its sprite made solid**, the way the reference builds one: the artwork extruded **one texel of its own grid** deep, with a wall raised on every boundary between a solid texel and an empty one. Those walls are the whole of it — they are what give a blade an edge and a handle a round side, and what makes the object read as a shape from every angle rather than only from the two flat ones. It was two bare quads a texel apart for a long time, which read as *two* swords side by side, because edge on there was a gap and nothing caught the light between them; the thickness had been correct since 2026-08-05 and the sides simply did not exist.

A wall samples its own texel at the **centre**, the same coordinate on all four corners. That carries the right colour, and it also pins the face to the sharpest mip level — a one-texel strip averaged down would fall under the cutout threshold and be discarded, so the object would go hollow as you walked away from it. A typical tool comes out around 60–80 walls, so roughly 300 triangles a drop.

The silhouette comes from `game::SpriteMask`, built once at startup from the alpha `engine::TextureArray` **keeps from its load** — about 46 KB for the whole sheet, against decoding every PNG a second time. The threshold is the fragment shader's own half-alpha, deliberately: a texel the shader would throw away has to count as absent here too, or a wall is left standing around a hole. `Renderer` hands the numbers out through `textureWidth`/`textureHeight`/`textureLayerCount`/`textureAlphaAt` rather than exposing the texture, so nothing outside the engine touches a Vulkan type to ask what shape a sprite cuts out.

Plants take the same path deliberately. In the ground a flower is two crossed quads, which is the shape it grows in; lying on the floor it is **one flower with real thickness**, exactly like everything else that has been dropped — the crossed pair read as two flowers passing through each other, which is the same complaint the sword had.

**A drop is 0.30 blocks across**, against the reference's quarter of a block. Larger on purpose — at the reference's size a dropped tool is hard to pick out of grass. It is the collision box as well as the model, so the two cannot disagree about how big the thing is.

Drops are **thrown**, not released: without a forward impulse a dropped stack lands at your feet and is collected again immediately. Each drop carries **its own pickup delay** — 0.35 s from breaking, 1.2 s when thrown — because the delay has to outlast the flight or the item is pulled straight back inside the 2 m attraction radius.

Landing **bounces**, keeping 42% of the impact speed, and anything slower than 2 m/s settles outright. That threshold is what makes it terminate; removing it to get a bouncier feel turns the animation into the infinite loop described in `CLAUDE.md`.

**A drop nobody collects is gone after five minutes.** Without that a long session accumulates every item it ever made, and each one rebuilds its geometry every frame. The reference pauses the timer when a chunk stops ticking; ours runs on wall time, which is simpler and equivalent because drops are not saved.

**Collection takes what fits rather than all or nothing.** `Inventory::add` returns whatever would not go in and the drop keeps exactly that, so a partial pickup was always supported — but the caller asked `hasRoomFor` for the *whole* stack first and skipped the drop entirely when it could not take all of it. Because the loop collects **one drop per frame** and stopped at the first stack it could not swallow whole, a single refused stack left every other drop in the world orbiting the player too. From the outside that looks like the pickup being broken rather than the inventory being nearly full, which is how it was reported. The arrow-recovery loop above it had the same shape and the same fix.

> ⛔ **`slots::roomFor` is the single owner of "how many of these may this stack accept", and it is `constexpr`.** `add`, `hasRoomFor`, `quickMove`, `gather` and `distribute` all count with it. Five separate answers existed before 2026-08-17 and three of them matched on `item` alone, so a worn pickaxe merged into a fresh one and a full stowbox merged into an empty one — both destroying whatever `damage` held. It answers zero for **anything that does not stack**, which is what turns a click of one tool onto another into a swap rather than a no-op; the reference swaps them, and a click that visibly does nothing reads as a broken screen. Four `static_assert`s state the rules, including the two that had been wrong.

`creative_mode` in `settings.cfg` keeps infinite blocks: placing never runs a stack down. **It changes nothing else.** Breaking drops, and drops are collected, in every mode — both halves of that were once suppressed in creative and both produced bugs, recorded in `CLAUDE.md`.

Stack counts are drawn in the **bottom-left** of a slot, and only when there is more than one — a count of one reads as simply having the thing.

### Crafting

`craftResult(slots, size)` returns what a grid currently makes, and `consumeIngredients` spends it. **They are separate calls because the result is a preview until it is taken** — the player sees what a grid would make, then decides.

A recipe's pattern is stored **at its own size**, not padded to the grid. The matcher finds the bounding box of the filled cells and compares the pattern against that, so a 1×2 recipe is craftable in either column of a 2×2 and anywhere in a 3×3. Since `craftResult` takes the grid size as an argument, a crafting table is a layout change rather than a matcher change.

Shapeless matching **counts leftovers**: after ticking off each ingredient it checks nothing else is in the grid, or a grid holding an extra item would still craft and quietly eat it.

Recipes live in one table in `item/Recipe.cpp` — **one thousand and nineteen of them**, four hundred and sixty of which fit a 2×2 so they are craftable without a table. **Most are generated in loops rather than written out**: eleven woods times eleven shared shapes, sixteen colours times three dyed families, five tool shapes times fourteen materials. Shapes and yields come from the reference recipe JSON; `CRAFTABLE.md` records every family and what is still missing.

> ⛔ **The tool helper broke the "stored at its own size" rule and cost sixteen recipes.** `tool()` draws each shape as a 3×3 picture and used to store it padded to 3×3, so the matcher — which compares against the *bounding box* of what is in the grid — could never match an axe, shovel, sword or hoe, every one of which leaves a column empty. Only the pickaxe filled all three columns, so it was the one craftable tool in the game and nothing else in the table was affected. It now trims the pattern to the cells it fills. **A rule written down in one place and re-implemented in a helper is the same second copy this codebase keeps paying for**, and the guard is cheap: feed every recipe's own pattern back through `craftResult` and assert it makes itself. Measured across all 340 — none broken, none shadowed by an earlier identical pattern.

> **Named divergence: a recipe cannot mix two woods.** The reference matches an item *tag*; `Recipe::pattern` holds concrete ids, and the craftable check explicitly relies on no ingredient naming a set. So the shared wooden recipes are generated once per wood, and four oak planks make a crafting table where two oak and two spruce do not.

Closing a screen **returns crafting ingredients** to the inventory, not just the cursor stack. Items left in a grid the player cannot see are items that quietly vanish.

### The crafting table

`BlockId::CraftingTable` answers `isInteractive`, which is what makes right-clicking it open a screen rather than place against it. Sneaking suppresses that, so a block can still be put down on top of one.

Its panel is **generated from the inventory panel** by `tools/make-hud-sheet.ps1`: same frame, same backdrop, same storage rows and hotbar, with the top section cleared and the *same 18×18 slot cell* stamped into a 3×3 and a result position. The cells are not a lookalike, they are the same pixels, so the two screens cannot drift apart. Positions came from measuring the reference GUI, which turned out to share our panel's rows exactly and differ by one pixel in its columns.

The matcher needed no changes at all — `craftResult` already took the grid size, and patterns are already stored at their own size.

### The furnace

**It faces the way you were looking when you placed it**, and only that side carries the mouth. The other three use `furnace_side` and the top and bottom use `furnace_top`, which is the reference's arrangement. It needed two things that did not exist: **`FaceDirection`**, so a side face can say which way it points - the mesher's face table already named all six, so it cost a column rather than a derivation - and **the facing stored in the block id**, the way stairs store their orientation.

`Furnace` and `FurnaceLit` stayed exactly where they were and became the north-facing pair; the other six ids are appended, because ids are what get written to disk. **`furnaceFacing` is the one place the facing and the lit state are combined**, so a furnace lighting up cannot quietly turn to face north - which is what a plain `lit ? FurnaceLit : Furnace` would have done. `blockLightEmission` asks `isFurnaceLit` rather than naming one id, or three of the four directions would have glowed for nobody.

The six new ids are **placement states, not items**: `isCanonicalBlockItem` asks `dropForBlock`, so the catalogue still lists exactly one furnace.

**The crafting table uses the same mechanism**, and needs no facing stored: the reference puts its tooled face on the two Z sides and a plainer one on the two X sides, fixed. It was returning the front on all four until `FaceDirection` existed to ask.

**An item icon has to supply a direction too, and that is not obvious.** The isometric icon draws *two* side faces at once, and they point different ways — so handing both `BlockFace::Side` with no direction showed a furnace's mouth on the right-hand face as well as the front, in the hotbar, the inventory and the catalogue alike. `blockFacing` gives the icon the block's own facing for the front quad and `quarterTurn` gives the right quad a plain side. Both answer `Unknown` for the great majority of blocks, which look the same all the way round, so every other icon is byte-identical.

**Smelting is two unrelated tables, and both grew up this round.** A recipe still takes **ten seconds**, but `kSmelting` is now **33 rows** — cobblestone → stone, stone → smooth stone, sand → glass, every raw metal → its ingot, the deepslate and nether ores, the foods, and **every log chars, not just the oak one**: the rule named a single id where `isLogBlock` already existed, so ten of the eleven woods could not make charcoal at all while `fuelBurnSeconds` beside it had asked the family predicate all along.

**Fuel is answered by family wherever a family exists, and by a named row only where one does not.** `kFuels` in `Smelting.cpp` holds 27 one-off rows — coal and charcoal 80 s, a block of coal 800, a dried kelp block 200, scaffolding and bamboo 2.5, saplings and azaleas and a dead bush 5, a stick 5, the five wooden tools 10, a fishing rod 15, bow, crossbow and bowl 10, a cinder rod 120, a lava bucket 1000. Everything else goes through `constexpr blockFuelSeconds`, which asks *shape* questions: planks and logs and bark and their stripped forms, then anything whose `shapedParent` is planks — which is what makes 640 stairs, slabs, fences, gates and walls fuel without naming one of them — then doors and trapdoors by family index, then the thin-wood families (signs, buttons, pressure plates, banners) at their own times. **All of it is per item in a plain furnace.**

- **Every number comes from the reference's Bedrock column, and three rows differ from Java.** Wooden and bamboo-mosaic slabs are 15 s on Bedrock against Java's 7.5 (MCPE-94368); a bow and a crossbow are 10 against Java's 15; a bowl is 10 against Java's 5, the one row where Bedrock is the *longer* of the two.
- **Wool and wool carpet are not fuel, because on Bedrock they are not.** The reference's fuel table marks both `{{only|je}}`. Leaving them out of `kFuels` was never enough on its own — the sixteen carpets were reaching the furnace through the family path, and were removed as a *consequence* of gating on `isPlanksBlock(shapedParent(block))` rather than by a subtraction list.
- **The gate is deliberately not `isFlammable`.** See `DECISIONS.md`; the short version is that the two predicates answer different questions and conflating them silently removed 612 blocks from this table.
- **A lava bucket is 1000 s and gives the bucket back.** `fuelRemainder` in `Smelting.hpp` maps `LavaBucket → Bucket` and `Furnace.cpp` puts it in the fuel slot instead of decrementing; a sweep there proves any fuel with a remainder has `maxStackFor == 1`, or the first of a pile would owe a container the slot has no room for.

**A smoker and a blast furnace are one multiplier, applied at the call site.** `Main.cpp` passes `deltaSeconds * cookSpeed(present)` into `tickFurnace`, and `cookSpeed` returns 2.0f for every smoker and blast-furnace id. **`tickFurnace` itself knows nothing about which cooker it is in**, which is the whole point: the reference cooks twice as fast *and* burns fuel twice as fast in those two, so items-per-fuel is unchanged, and one multiplier on the whole tick is the only arrangement that gets both halves right. Two independent rates would have been wrong, and a second 2× inside `tickFurnace` would have produced a **4× smoker** — which is what implementing the obvious-looking version of that finding would have done. `kSmeltSeconds` and every row of `kFuels` are therefore **cooker seconds, not wall-clock**; `cookSeconds(BlockId)` in `Smelting.hpp` is where the wall-clock answer lives.

**Fuel is only lit when there is something worth cooking**, so a furnace loaded with charcoal and nothing else sits cold instead of quietly burning through it. Cook progress slides back rather than resetting, so pulling an item out for a moment does not throw away its cooking.

**Lit and unlit are two different blocks.** `Furnace` and `FurnaceLit` differ in their front texture and in the light they cast (13), and both of those are properties of the block itself — the same reasoning that puts water levels and stair facings in the id.

**The contents are a block entity**, which is the thing the id trick cannot do. They live in a map keyed by block position in `Main.cpp`, not in `World`: chunks are loaded and saved on worker threads, and there is no reason to route block-entity data through that. The cost is that they are written on world save rather than when a chunk unloads, and that entries outlive their chunk being unloaded — both cheap for something a player places a handful of. They persist to `furnaces.dat` beside `player.dat`, and the record is `static_assert`ed trivially copyable because it is written as raw bytes.

**A furnace's output slot is storage, not a preview.** Unlike a crafting result you can only take from it, never put into it, so the shared click handling branches there and nowhere else.

Both progress indicators are the **lit sprite drawn over the spent one** baked into the panel, clipped to how far along the furnace is: the flame is cut from the top because it burns downward, the arrow from the right because it fills rightward.

**Known gap:** a furnace's lit state lives in the block and its contents live in `furnaces.dat`, so if that file is lost or rejected the block stays lit forever with nothing behind it. Opening it creates a fresh entry and the next tick puts it out. Not worth architecture to prevent, but worth knowing when a furnace looks stuck.

### Mining and tools

> ⚠️ **Everything in this section, and in "Items and drops", "Chest loot" and the drop half of "Dying", landed overnight on 2026-08-17/18 and has never been played.** Both presets build clean at `/W4`, a 45-second soak reports zero validation errors and zero stderr, and the tables are held by `constexpr` sweeps — which between them prove that it compiles, that no row is missing and that it does not crash. **They say nothing about whether a break *feels* right or a haul *reads* right.** The drop-rate figures below come from throwaway statistical probes over the tables, not from a player breaking anything.

**One row per block id, and `game/src/item/Mining.hpp` owns it.** `MiningRow{hardness, tool, tier, toolRequired}` is eight bytes, `kMiningRows` is a `std::array` sized by `kBlockIdCount`, and every answer is **one field of one read** off `miningRow`. ⚠️ **Corrected 2026-08-19:** this used to read "`blockHardness`, `harvestTool`, `harvestTier` and `yieldsDrop` are each one field of one read (`Tool.cpp`, six one-line functions onto `miningRow`)". `Tool.cpp` now holds **three** forwarders — `toolFor`, `blockHardness`, `yieldsDrop` — because `harvestTool`, `harvestTier` and `breakSecondsGrounded` were deleted the same day for having zero callers. Ask `miningRow(block).tool` and `.tier` directly. It replaced four hand-written accessors that each carried their own range tests over the seven table runs — and they had drifted apart exactly as that arrangement guarantees: one covered extra run 7 and the others did not, one gave a redstone block a wood tier and another a hand tier, and forty-three ids in run 1 sat behind a tier no tool accessor named a kind for, so a fist opened them.

**The table is built by walking the enum**, in **256-id chunks** because deriving all `kBlockIdCount` rows in one constant expression exceeds MSVC's million-step budget. Each chunk is its own `constexpr` variable with its own budget, and the flat table is a copy of the folded constants. ⚠️ **The chunk *count* is derived and the chunk *list* is not, and that gap is load-bearing — it was the subject of a fix at 10:23:32 on 2026-08-19 that is worth copying.** Until then one constant did both jobs: the pointer array was sized by `kMiningChunkCount` and held **thirteen** hand-written pointers, so the margin between the enum and a build failure was whatever `3328 − kBlockIdCount` happened to be that hour — measured at **nineteen ids**, with two other agents appending block runs the same evening. **Note what the failure would have been:** aggregate initialisation does not object to *too few* initialisers, it value-initialises the rest, so a fourteenth slot would have been a null `MiningChunk*` that `makeMiningRows` dereferences for every id from 3,328 up. The `static_assert` was the only thing making that a build error instead. **And the obvious repair was a trap** — adding a thirteenth chunk and bumping the assert to `== 14` breaks the build *immediately* on a tree still under 3,328, because the array would be sized 13 by the derived count and handed 14 initialisers, which unlike too few is a hard error. **The fix was to split the constant:** `kMiningChunkCount` is what the enum needs, `kMiningChunkCapacity` is what is written, the assert is `<=`, and a second assert pins the capacity against the chunks actually written so raising one number alone cannot silence it (bug shape #11 — an assert comparing one side of a derivation against itself). ⭐ **That control was rewritten again within the hour and the reason is worth more than the fix.** Its first form compared pointers — `kMiningChunks[kMiningChunkCapacity - 1] == &kMiningChunk13` — which is sound C++ on paper but is **precisely the shape MSVC is narrowest about in a constant expression**. The replacement, `chunkPointersMapToTheirBases()`, **compares the values the pointers yield** instead: it walks every chunk the table can reach and checks row 0 against the row that base derives, all four fields rather than one because `tier` alone collides freely. It still catches a null slot (dereferencing one is ill-formed in a constant expression) and a mis-wired slot, it is non-vacuous by construction, and it reuses character for character an expression `makeMiningRows` already evaluates — **so it cannot fail for a reason that would not also have broken the table**. Copy that property, not the syntax. The ceiling is now **3,584**, roughly **275 ids** of headroom over the last probe of 3,309, and a spare chunk costs nothing while unused because both loops stop at `kBlockIdCount`.

> ⭐ **Sized by the enum guarantees a row exists; the sentinel is what guarantees somebody chose it.** The final `default:` returns `kUnchosenHardness` / `kUnchosenTool` — a row that *cannot* be self-consistent — and the fifth sweep invariant fails the build naming the id. Without it a newly appended run of a hundred rock ids came out hardness 1.0, no tool, hand tier, and passed all four of the sweep's original invariants, because each of them was conditioned on a tier above hand, on a tool being required, or on a hardness at or below zero. That is the difference between a build error and a playtest finding, and the earlier claim that "sized by the enum" already achieved it was wrong.

**The break formula is Bedrock's own, in Bedrock's own order**, and it was Java-shaped until now:

1. `speed = isBestTool ? tool.speed : 1` — the wrong **kind** of tool is worth exactly a fist however good it is.
2. **`if (!canHarvest) speed = 1`** — the Bedrock line Java dropped in 1.5. Without it the speed and the divisor were picked by two independent tests.
3. Haste and Mining Fatigue, when the caller passes a `speedScale`, multiplied in **before** the rounding.
4. **÷5 for a submerged head** (we have no Aqua Affinity to exempt it) and **÷5 again for feet off the ground**. Both at once is 25× slower.
5. `damage = speed / hardness / (canHarvest ? 30 : 100)`; `damage >= 1` is an instant break, which also skips the six-tick cooldown and the tool's wear.
6. **`ceil` to whole ticks**, because a tick is the unit the reference counts in — a 22.5-tick break costs 23.

`underwater` and `onGround` are facts about the *player*, so they are parameters rather than defaults; `breakSecondsGrounded` in `Tool.hpp` is the two-argument spelling and **states its assumption in its own name**, which is what stops a future caller believing it asked the general question.

**`canHarvest` is kind *and* tier**, which the old body could not express — it compared tiers with a single exception for shears, so an Emberite shovel collected diamond ore and a fist collected a block of iron. A cobweb is the third shape: the reference declares no best tool for it and *still* withholds it from a bare hand, which is why it is 20 s by hand rather than 6 s — no tool means the unharvestable divisor.

**Twenty-odd `static_assert`s check the whole expression against the reference's published times**, both sides `constexpr` so none of it can rot: stone by hand 150 ticks, stone with a wooden pickaxe 23, iron ore with a wooden pickaxe **300** (15.0 s, where the old formula gave 7.5 s), obsidian with a diamond pickaxe 188, a gold block by hand 300, a cobweb by hand 400, and stone with a wooden pickaxe underwater-and-airborne 563.

**What the correction moved, measured over the id space rather than estimated.** **291 block ids changed harvest requirement** — 290 tighter and exactly one looser, mangrove leaves. The iron, gold, diamond, emerald, lapis and copper blocks were punchable by hand *for a full drop*, and **152 stair, slab and wall ids inherited the same hole through `shapedParent`**. **860 ids now refuse the wrong tool kind** where none did before. **100 self-parented ids had silently defaulted to hardness 1.0** — 16 concretes, 16 terracottas, the whole wool family (so a carpet took 1.5 s by hand against 0.15 s), the deepslate variants and the prismarines; the iron, diamond and emerald blocks were priced at 3.0 against the reference's 5.0.

**The tier demand is still the whole progression**, and it is now a decision for every id rather than a default for four of the seven runs: rock withholds its drop, everything else comes away bare-handed, and a block that demands a *kind* at any tier — a vine wanting shears, an amethyst cluster wanting a pickaxe — says so on its own row rather than through a tier comparison that cannot express it. **Creative pays no time cost, no wear and always drops**, which is the one place mode is allowed to matter besides placing.

**Five tiers**, and their speeds and durabilities are the reference's own rather than invented: wood 2× and 60 uses, stone 4× and 132, **iron 6× and 250, diamond 8× and 1561, Emberite 9× and 2031**. `kTools` moved into `Mining.hpp` with everything else, so the whole break formula is `constexpr` and provable at compile time; `toolFor` is one line onto it. A sword's number is deliberately smaller than its tier's mining speed, because a sword is not a mining tool — the reference gives it a flat 1.5× on everything and scales the *blow* with the material instead, and `strike` reads that same field for damage. Wear is counted per block broken and only on blocks that resist — plants and torches cost nothing, and so does anything the formula finishes inside one tick. **Tools do not stack**, because two with different wear are not interchangeable, which is why `maxStackFor` exists rather than a bare `kMaxStack`.

**`isTool` spans two runs of item ids and has to.** The upper three tiers were appended at the very end of the item list rather than beside the wood and stone tools, because an item id is written into the player's saved inventory and inserting there would have turned every spawn egg, resource and bucket in a saved world into something else. Missing the second run in that predicate does not fail — it makes fifteen tools stack, never wear out, and mine like a fist.

**Emberite is ours, and it is the one tier you cannot make from raw material.** The reference's name is coined and needs replacing; *ancient*, *debris*, *scrap* and *ingot* are ordinary English and stay. Ancient debris is the rarest vein in the ground, about five times scarcer than diamond and in the same deep band; it smelts to scrap, four scrap and four gold make an ingot, and an ingot plus a **diamond tool** makes the Emberite one. The reference upgrades at a smithing table with a template; we have neither, so the upgrade is a shapeless pair — which keeps what the tier means without a new screen. Its ore does not avoid air the way the reference's does, because that rule exists to stop it being spotted across a lava lake and we have no lava.

Dig progress is drawn as a bar under the crosshair. The HUD only rebuilds when asked, so the frame digging *stops* has to ask too — otherwise the last bar drawn stays on screen forever, which is exactly what happened first time.

### Torches

A torch is a **2×10×2 stick**, the reference's own `template_torch`: one model box whose walls sample the lower ten rows of the image and whose lid samples the two rows the flame sits on. It emits light 14 and, like plants, needs something solid beneath it — placing without support is refused, and breaking that support drops it.

It was two crossed sheets until 2026-08-10, which is what a *plant* is, and it also selected as a whole cube because `blockShape` had no model for it. **`postBoxes` is what the crosshair and the collision test read**, and a torch's is 7/16–9/16 across and ten sixteenths tall, so the outline hugs the stick. A `static_assert` holds that.

**Wall torches are deliberately absent.** They need either a tilted box or an offset cross plus four orientations in the block id, and floor torches light a cave perfectly well in the meantime.

## Staying Alive

Built at M21. `world/Survival.hpp` is the single owner of every number named here; the sequence below is what actually happens each frame, in `updateSurvival` at the end of `updatePlayer`.

**Damage does not use a plain cooldown, and the difference matters.** For half a second after being hit you are invulnerable — but a *bigger* blow inside that window still lands, for the difference between it and the one already taken. Without that rule an ordinary punch would absorb the creeper standing next to you. RESEARCH §2.4 owns the reasoning; the worked example there (7 damage, then 12 in the same window, lands 5 more) is what the implementation is checked against.

**Hunger drains by exhaustion, not by time.** Every action has a cost — a sprinted metre, a jump, a broken block, a landed blow — and four points of accumulated exhaustion spends one leg of the food bar. Standing still costs nothing at all, which is why a bar that only ticks down on a timer feels wrong and this does not.

What the bar then gates:

| Food | What happens |
|---|---|
| 18 or more | Health regenerates, one point every four seconds |
| 18 or more **with saturation left** | Every half second instead, at a cost of 1.5 saturation a time |
| Below 6 | Sprinting is refused |
| 0 | Starvation, one point every four seconds, stopping at half a heart |

**Saturation is a hidden buffer above the visible bar**, filled by eating and spent before hunger is. It is clamped to the current food level, which is what stops a steak eaten at 19/20 banking twelve invisible points.

Hazards, all of them on their own timers so leaving one stops the damage immediately: falling more than three blocks (one point a block), drowning, suffocating inside a solid block, standing in fire or lava, still burning for a few seconds after stepping out, touching a cactus, and falling out of the world below Y −8.

**Eating is held, not clicked** — 1.6 seconds with the right button down, and a full bar refuses outright. Thirty-three foods carry a hunger value and a saturation value.

Dying drops the whole inventory where you stood and respawns you 1.6 seconds later. Creative mode is immune to all of it, which arrives through `PlayerInput::invulnerable` rather than by the survival code knowing what mode the game is in.

**Where you land is `World::groundHeight`, and it is the single owner.** Fresh spawn, the lift a resumed save gets when the terrain moved under it, and respawning after death all ask it. It is deliberately *not* `highestSolid() + 1`, which is what all three used to write: `highestSolid` answers −1 for a column no chunk is loaded for, and −1 + 1 is the bottom of the world. `groundHeight` falls back to the generator's `surfaceHeightAt`, which is always available and is the right answer for ground nobody has touched.

> ⛔ **The player must ask `columnResident` before it falls, and climb out if it is inside rock.** Both rules were written for creatures the day creatures were written, with the reasoning spelled out in `Creature.cpp` — *"an absent chunk reads as air, so simulating over one drops the creature out of the world and it reappears buried when the chunk returns"* — and `updatePlayer` was never given either of them. Respawning at a world spawn you have since walked away from is the way in: the column is gone, so you are placed at the bottom of the world, or you free-fall through empty air until the chunks arrive and bury you at whatever depth you had reached. Both now live at the top of `updatePlayer`, in that order.
