## Projectiles

`world/Projectile.hpp/.cpp`. Five kinds - the arrow, the thrown pearl, the thrown egg and the two thrown potions - and a `ProjectileSpecies` table, because a second copy of a launch speed is the recurring bug here.

> ⛔ **Every number is per *tick*, and `Projectiles::update` runs a fixed twenty-hertz accumulator because of it.** Multiplying by an inertia of 0.99 once a frame at 120 fps is six times the intended drag. The fixed step is also what buys the cheapest real check available: the closed form `v(t) = k^t (v₀ + g/(1−k)) − g/(1−k)` holds *exactly*, and a temporary probe measured the drift at 1e-6 over forty ticks. **Do not convert this to `deltaSeconds`.**

> ⛔ **What is *drawn* is interpolated between ticks, and that is not optional either.** Twenty positions a second on a screen doing 120 shows each one for six frames, which is exactly what the user reported as "very very rough". Every shot keeps its `previousPosition` and `previousHeading` from the last tick, and `buildMesh` blends toward the current pair by `accumulator / tick`. That is one tick of latency, invisible, and it leaves the simulation untouched — measured frame by frame, the drawn x now advances on every frame in proportion to the frame time. **Fix smoothness in the renderer, never by raising the tick rate**, or every published constant above stops meaning what it says.

Per tick, in this order — **position, then drag, then gravity**: `position += velocity; velocity *= inertia; velocity.y -= gravity`. The order is provable rather than a guess: it gives a terminal speed of `g/(1−k)` = 5.00 blocks a tick, where dragging the acceleration too would give 4.95, and the reference publishes 5.00 for an arrow and 4.95 for a thrown potion. A `static_assert` holds it.

- Arrow: `power` 3.0 b/t, `gravity` 0.05 b/t², `inertia` 0.99 air / 0.6 water, box 0.25.
- Void pearl: `power` 1.5, `gravity` 0.025, **`inertia` and `liquid_inertia` both exactly 1** - the reference overrides the thrown-item family's defaults, so a pearl has no drag and no terminal speed at all. That is why it reaches 45 blocks thrown straight up where a snowball reaches 28, and a `static_assert` on `v²/2g` holds it.
- Egg: `power` 1.5, `gravity` 0.03, and the family's own 0.99 / 0.6 drag. Two rows rather than one "thrown item", because those are the numbers that differ.
- Splash and lingering potion: `power` **0.5** - they are lobbed rather than thrown - and the 0.05 gravity that gives the 4.95 terminal speed the order-of-operations assert above is calibrated against. **Their `item` is `None`**, because forty-one brews share each row: which one this is rides on the shot as `payload`, and comes back out on the landing.
- Neither thrown item damages anything: `damagePerSpeed` of zero is the reference's `impact_damage: null`, and it is also what makes them skip the creature sweep entirely. **Named divergence:** the reference stops them on entities and ours do not.
- **A thrown item is drawn as the same solid object it would be lying on the floor**: its sprite extruded a texel deep with a wall on every boundary between a solid texel and an empty one, built by `appendSpriteModel` in `item/SpriteModel.hpp` — the one function a dropped item uses. Two crossed flat quads read as two pearls passing through each other. It is billboarded toward the camera, which is what the reference's own thrown-item renderer does, and drawn at the dropped item's own half-extent so the two are the same size. Measured: 54 quads and a thickness of exactly one sprite texel.
- `reportsImpact` puts a landing on a queue the owner drains, exactly as `Creatures::takeLoot` does - this system reads the world and never writes it, and has no idea a player or a roster exists. A pearl moves the thrower; an egg leaves a chick one throw in eight, and four one throw in thirty-two.
- **The player is a target through a callback, not through a pointer.** `Projectiles::tick` took the creature roster and nothing else until 2026-08-17, so a skeleton's, a stray's, a bogged's or a Blackbone's arrow **could never hit you at all** — they were decoration for as long as archers had existed. A `PlayerReach` callable answers "is the player's box on this segment", and a hit goes onto a queue `takePlayerHits()` drains, on the same hand-off `takeLoot` uses. It is **damage only: there is no knockback**, because Bedrock publishes no sourced figure for an arrow's shove and inventing one is the wrong-unit bug this project has already paid for twice. The callback is also what keeps a screen honest — a shot cannot land on a player standing in an open inventory unless it is their own arrow.
- **Every shot carries who fired it, and both ends of that had to be got right.** `strike` takes a `fromId` and an `ignoreId`, so an arrow that hits a bystander blames the archer rather than the player — a mob's stray shot into your wolf used to turn the pack on you. **The fix then inverted the bug onto the player**, because the two places the *player's* own arrows are launched kept the defaulted owner: unknown owner means "blame the player", the sweep skips whoever is being blamed, and the player's arrows passed straight through every mob within about fifteen blocks. Both sites now pass `Projectiles::kPlayerOwner` explicitly. **A defaulted parameter is how a caller keeps the old behaviour**; `LESSONS.md` carries the shape.
- **A splash potion applies its brew where it lands**, to everyone inside four blocks and weaker the further out they are; a lingering one leaves a **cloud** instead, which shrinks over thirty seconds and applies a quarter strength once a second. Both are applied by the owner, for the reason above - `lingeringClouds` is a plain vector in `Main.cpp` and holds a handful at a time.
- **A pearl lands the player where it stopped, or does not land them at all.** The body is wider and taller than the 0.25 pearl, so the cell it stopped in is a starting guess: the exact point, then the middle of that cell, then the same two a block higher, up to three blocks. A throw with nowhere to stand is spent without moving you rather than melding you into the wall. Cooldown 1 s, the reference's own.
- **The reference publishes no in-air limit for a thrown item**, checked against `ender_pearl.json` (no `minecraft:despawn`, no timer) - so both fall under the same 60 s cap the arrow has.
- **Blocks are swept before entities**, and the segment is clamped to the block hit before anything is asked about what is standing there — the other order lets an arrow hit something behind a wall. `sweepBlocks` in `Raycast.hpp` is a **third question for the one walker**, reading `collisionBoxes`; `raycast` reads `selectionBoxes` and was deliberately not widened.
- **Damage is `ceil(2 × current speed)`**, never the launch speed. Rounded up *before* the critical roll, which the reference has an explicit flag for. A fully charged shot crits.
- Owner immunity is 5 ticks — a window, not a permanent exemption.
- A landed arrow sticks, wobbles for 0.35 s on pitch alone, is collectable if a player fired it in survival, and expires after 60 s. **A mob's arrow is never collectable**, even in creative, or a skeleton is an arrow farm.
- The model is the reference's: two flat quads crossed through the shaft plus a nock square. The fletching is *painted*, not modelled. Its 32×32 sheet is cropped to its top-left sixteenth rather than resized, because a texture array needs every layer the same size.

**The bow.** `bowCharge(seconds)` is the reference's quadratic `(f² + 2f)/3`, and four `static_assert`s pin it to the four rows of the reference's own published damage table. Below `kMinBowCharge` nothing fires — no arrow spent, no wear taken. `bowPullStage` picks the icon and **finishes in half the time the charge does**, which is the reference's own split; it must never decide the shot. Durability 385, spent per arrow fired. Firing happens on the button's **falling edge**, so the main loop keeps `bowHeld` from the previous frame. The three drawn-bow pictures are the *artwork* of the pull; what fills the gaps between them is the hotbar icon **shrinking on the charge curve, dead centre in its slot** — it reads as the bow being drawn back away from you, and a fraction of the icon's own size is a limit by construction. Sliding it back along the arrow's axis was tried and read as the bow slipping into the corner of the slot.

> ⛔ **A drawing bow has to be in the HUD's rebuild condition.** `hudDirty` is set when the draw starts and when it ends, so without `|| bowHeld` the hotbar is built once at the beginning of the pull and not again until the arrow leaves — the picture and the size are computed correctly every frame and never uploaded. Same shape as the dig bar this replaced; the condition names all four continuous cases.

> ⛔ **There is deliberately no first-person view of the held item.** One was built and removed the same day: the user's whole reaction to it was *"the hell is this grass block in the bottom right corner?? remove it."* The request it answered was that the bow's three-frame pull looked choppy, and the fix belonged in the slot the bow already occupies.

### Two screen layers, plus a third for the cursor

`setScreenMesh`, then `setClippedScreenMesh` (scissored, for the catalogue's cut last row), then `setTopScreenMesh`. The third exists because **a blended fragment still writes depth**: the stack on the cursor was nearest of everything in the inventory mesh, and the catalogue icons are a separate draw that comes after it, so wherever the held artwork was transparent it had already stamped its depth and punched a rectangular hole through the list behind it. Ordering is the only fix while the HUD shares the world pipeline. The top layer carries the carried stack and its tooltip, and is empty whenever no screen is open.

**Archers.** `CreatureSpecies::shootsArrows` is the other half of the split `swingsArms` already recorded: skeleton, stray and bogged. `RangedAttack` is a real behaviour row at priority 4, above `MeleeAttack` and claiming the same controllers, and `meleeAttackStart` refuses an archer outright so neither the tie nor the ordering is load-bearing alone. It backs off inside 4 m, closes outside 9 m, and looses once a second at Bedrock's `mob_arrow` power of 1.6 with the Normal-difficulty spread of 8. `Creatures::takeLaunches()` hands the shot over rather than firing it — the same arrangement as `takeLoot`.

> ⭐ **`Projectiles::takeCreatureStrikes()` is the return leg of that hand-off, and it closes the loop the other way.** An arrow that hits a creature is resolved by `Projectiles`, which knows nothing about health, herds or anger; the strike — who was hit, by how much, and **who fired it** — comes back as a list the frame loop applies. Carrying the shooter is the whole point: it is what lets `Creatures::rouse` blame the right party, and what stopped a skeleton's stray arrow turning a wolf pack on the player.

## Ladders, vines and the third table run

`WhiteStainedGlass..EndRod` is a **third** table-driven run, appended for the reason the second exists: everything before it is on disk. Sixteen stained glass, iron bars, both lanterns, the soul and redstone torches and the end rod.

### Glass, and where its transparency actually lives

**In the art, and nowhere else.** `tinted_glass.png` is a frame at alpha 200 around a centre panel at 110; a stained glass is a frame at 163, a diagonal highlight streak at 155 and a panel at 102. Those three levels *are* the block: they are what make a border read as a border and a panel read as tinted.

- **Staging must not flatten them**, and `make-reference-blocks.ps1` names them beside water, the sun and the moon for that reason. Its shape test — no fully clear texel, most texels partly clear — reads glass as translucent block art and would otherwise rewrite all 256 texels to opaque. Ice, honey and slime still go through it and should.
- **`kDrawFlagBlended` exempts the blended pass from the cutout alpha test.** That test throws away anything under half alpha, which would keep a glass frame and its streak and delete the panel. It is safe to skip exactly there because a blended fragment does not write depth, which is what the test protects.
- **`translucentAlpha` answers 1.0 for glass** and `kWaterAlpha` for water. Water is the other way round — its art is opaque and the vertex is the whole of its transparency.
- **The seventeen blended ids include the sixteen stained panes.** A pane is a `ShapedFamily` on the block, so it wears the block's own texture layer; left on the cutout path it would draw as a frame with a hole. `isBlendedGlass` is declared below `kPaneFamilies` purely so it can ask.
- **A dropped glass block travels with them.** `ItemEntities::buildMesh` takes a second mesh for exactly this — the drop is the fourth place a block is drawn, and the one this change would otherwise have left as a wireframe cube on the floor. The inventory icon needed nothing: the HUD shader blends and has never had the alpha test.

> ⛔ **This is what the user reported as "it looks like a ghost".** Flattening the art and then painting the whole face with one averaged number — 0.46, or 0.51 for tinted — is uniform mush with no border, no streak and no panel. Three layers had all agreed that transparency rides on the vertex; it does not.

> ⛔ **An undead caught in daylight burns to death rather than being deleted.** It used to be retired outright the moment the sky light reached twelve, which meant a zombie from a spawn egg at noon **vanished on the frame it appeared** - no fire, no body, no drop, and nothing to tell the player what had happened. It now takes the reference's own fire damage, one point a second above sky light twelve, so it staggers, flashes, falls over and leaves what it was carrying; a zombie therefore has about twenty seconds to reach shade. Water and shade both put it out, and shade **resets** the count rather than pausing it. That is also what makes **anything spawnable in daylight** - the ones the sun kills simply take the time it takes.

A **ladder** spends four ids on which wall it is fixed to, and takes that facing from *where it landed* rather than from the camera — it is the one placed block whose orientation is a fact about the world. It has **no collision box at all** (a ladder you bump into is one you cannot get onto), so `selectionBoxes` answers with its drawn rungs or it would be unbreakable, and `Player::climbableAt` tests whole cells rather than shape or nothing would ever climb.

**Vines are sixteen ids, one per combination of the four sides they cling to.** That is Bedrock's own `vine_direction_bits`; Java spends a fifth bit on the sheet under a ceiling, and Bedrock derives that from whether anything is above — so the mesher asks the world for it and sixteen ids cover the block completely. `placeVine` **merges** a side into whatever is already there, which is the whole reason those sixteen exist: a cell between two trunks clings to both. Drawn double-sided, because a vine sheet is seen from either face.

**Only shears collect a vine**, and no tier comparison can say that — so `ToolKind::Shears` exists and `yieldsDrop` asks what *kind* of tool is held when `harvestTool` names it. Shears are deliberately no faster than a bare hand; the axe is the quick tool. Vines burn, are washed away by water, and are `isReplaceable`.

**Cocoa** is four facings times three ages, so the facing is the offset within a triple and the age is which triple. It hangs off the side of a jungle log with the top of the pod a quarter of a block below the top of the log at every age, which is what makes a row of them line up. Ripe gives three beans, younger gives one, and the beans are the reference's brown dye.

> ⛔ **Cocoa has to be placed before the trunk vines, not after.** A cell already holding a vine refuses a pod, and the trunk is 75 % vined — putting cocoa second meant not one tree in the world carried a pod, and nothing anywhere reported it.

Climbing **replaces** gravity rather than fighting it, the same rule water follows, and you climb by **pushing into** the block rather than by moving at all: strafing along a wall has no component into it, so A and D move you sideways instead of hauling you up. A vine with no side at all — a curtain hanging from the one above — is climbed from any direction. Jump climbs, sneak holds you still, and letting go slides you down at 1.4 m/s.

### Modelled blocks

Every other shape here is *cut out of a cube*, so where a box sits in its cell is also where it samples the texture — right for a stair, a slab or a fence, and wrong for a lantern, whose six-texel body is painted in the corner of a 16×48 sheet. `ModelBox` carries **its own texture rectangles** beside its extent - one for the four walls and a second for the lid, because a net paints those in different places and reusing the wall rect put the lantern's glass on its top and squashed its cap's plate into a sliver. `postModel` holds the reference's own `template_lantern`, `end_rod` and `cocoa_stage2` geometry, face rectangle for face rectangle. The mesher uses that rect when a shape has a model and derives one from position otherwise, and `appendBlockIcon` draws the same boxes isometrically - which is what makes an end rod's slot picture a rod rather than a two-texel sliver.

The lantern's handle is the reference's two crossed quads, a texel thick and crossing at a right angle where the reference turns them 45°, because the box mesher has no rotation. The hole through the middle of each is the artwork's own transparency, which works because a lantern is a cutout block. Its collision and selection are the reference's body alone, 5-11 across and 0-7 tall.

> ⛔ **A face is buried only when *all* of it is.** The mesher probed the centre of a face against the block's other boxes, which is right for a stair's step and wrong for a lantern - the cap covers the middle of the body's lid and leaves a one-texel ring showing all round, and the ring vanished. Five probes now: the centre and the four corners pulled a hundredth inward.

**A box may name its own texture layer**, `sideLayer` for the walls and `lidLayer` for the lid, or -1 to take the block's own. A bell is a stone frame with a plank bar round a gold bell and a grindstone is a stone wheel between two log legs: one block painted from several images. Without it a model could pick its rectangle but not its picture, and every post came out gold.

> ⛔ **`ModelBox::lidTurnsFacing` is the single owner of "this lid marks a world direction", and for twenty milestones the bed was the only block that set it.** A lid texture that is not radially symmetric has to be turned with the block, or three facings out of four wear it sideways or backwards — which is exactly what a repeater and a comparator did, both carrying their torch sockets painted along one axis. Every horizontal user now **derives the quarter-turn count from this flag** rather than writing four cases out again, and the same field serves the reference's own per-face `"rotation"` key. This is bug shape #5 in one field: a derivation applied to one of a pair and not the other.

> ⛔ **`ExtraBlockInfo::layer` is an offset into the appended run, not a layer index.** `blockTextureLayer` adds `kTableSpritesFirst` to it. Eleven constants beside the models were written as the row's bare number, which pointed the whole family at nether plants — a lily pad for the brewing stand's rod, weeping vines for the bell — and **the `static_assert`s still passed**, because each compared the offset against the offset and never once checked the sum. The base is now stated once as `kTableLayerBase`, asserted once against `kTableSpritesFirst`, and every constant is derived from it.

**Two things a lid and a wall need saying about direction, because the box mesher cannot rotate a model.**

- `lidTurns` is quarter turns applied to the lid. The top face's u runs along +X and its v along +Z, so an unturned head texture puts a bed's pillow at −Z whichever way the bed lies; three of the four facings had the pillow against the join in the middle instead of at the end.
- `unmirror` names one side face whose automatic U flip is to be undone. The mesher flips U on half the faces so a texture reads the same way from every side, which is what a word or a furnace front wants and exactly wrong for a texture that marks a *world* direction. A bed's side is red mattress at the join and white pillow at the head, so the flip put the pillow at the wrong end on precisely one of the two long sides.

The bed is drawn from that machinery rather than as a plate: a mattress box at y 3–9 and two 3×3 legs at y 0–3 on the half's outer end, so the pair of halves stands on four. **Its side texture is a net, not a face** — rows 0–7 transparent, 7–13 the mattress and frame, 13–16 three leg faces packed side by side — so sampling from row 0 drew mostly nothing and no legs at all.

> ⛔ **Its top texture is the opposite: one whole face, and treating it as a net is what broke it.** The reference's `template_bed_head` samples `up` at uv 0,0–16,16 over the entire cell, and the head image is pillow in rows 0–7, the shadow the pillow casts in row 8 and blanket in rows 9–15. Cropping the head's lid rect to the pillow stretched it over the whole head half and left the blanket nowhere, so the red began at the join instead of covering the middle of the bed. With the full rect and `lidTurns`, the pillow is half a block at the outer end and the other three quarters of the bed is blanket. **Row 8 is a dark red line, not a transparent slit** — `tools/dump-pixels.ps1` says so in one command, and the guess that it was a separator is what put the crop there.

> ⛔ **The head's outward end face has a texture of its own, `bed_head_north.png`, shared by all sixteen colours.** It is the pillow's own end and is white across the whole mattress band. Drawing it from the long-side image instead — which is half pillow, half blanket — painted the headboard red down one half and white down the other. `blockTextureLayer` answers it before the row's own layer is reached for, the way the furnace's mouth is answered.

> ⛔ **We stage one side image per half where the reference ships a mirrored pair, and that is why `unmirror` exists — and why the legs moved.** `*_bed_foot_east.png` packs its two leg faces at u 0–9 and `*_bed_head_east.png` packs its at u 7–16. Reading the foot's corner for both left the head's legs sampling empty texture and every bed in the world stood on two. `legU` is the one number that says which corner a half reads from.

### Every block is checked against the reference's own model

`block_probe=1` in `settings.cfg` writes **`block-shapes.txt`** beside the exe — one line per block id giving its shape and the box its drawn geometry actually occupies — and exits without opening a window. **`tools/check-models.ps1` runs that, reads the reference's `models/block/*.json`, and names every block whose measurements disagree by more than half a texel.** It is to block models exactly what `worldgen_probe` is to terrain, and it exists because the most expensive bug shape on this project is a rectangle or an extent guessed out of a picture instead of read from the model that states it.

**Current reading (2026-08-19): 3230 blocks drawn, 2629 matched a reference model and agree, 0 disagree, 271 have no model to check against.** Of those 271, **202** are blocks the reference draws as a block entity and ships no geometry for, **69** it ships only as a single face template, and **0** are blocks we failed to find a model for at all. Two stronger checks run beside the extents: **359 `Model` blocks compared box for box, 0 disagreeing on how many**, and **95 face rectangles read out of `postModel` in `Block.hpp` and compared against the `uv` the reference states, 0 disagreeing**. The remaining drawn blocks are divergences the tool names and explains in two sections of its own output — ones that are deliberate, and ones whose whole difference is a turned or paper-thin element a box mesher cannot express. A further 29 boxes in `postModel` could not be read statically, because they sit behind a switch, a loop or a variable, and 5 more had no element in the same place to compare against; **neither group is counted as agreeing**, which is the honest way round.

**The history of this number is the most useful thing about it.** It read **1792 matched / 0 disagreeing / 1370 with no model** for weeks. Then it read **2539 / 275**. Now it reads 2629 / 0.

- **The 275 was the tool ceasing to be blind, not the geometry getting worse.** Until then it compared *union extents only* — the outer box of what we draw against the outer box the reference describes. Two real bugs walked straight through that: a flower pot whose two X walls carried the whole pot's lid rect, and a scaffolding missing its four top rails. Neither moves a union extent by a texel. Adding the box count and the `uv` comparison surfaced 275 faults that had been present, and passing, all along.
- **The 1370 "no model" falling to 271 is the same story from the other side.** The tool had been giving up whenever the first filename it tried did not match, so most of the game sat in an unmeasured bucket that looked like an acceptable cost. Teaching it to follow variants, templates and block-entity cases moved 1099 blocks from "not checked" to "checked and agreeing", and left a residue of 271 that it can now *name a reason for*.

**The lesson for anyone about to improve a checker: expect the fault count to go up, and do not read that as having broken something.** A checker that reports zero because it is not looking is worse than one that reports 275, because the first one is trusted.

Four things the tool had to learn before its output meant anything, and each is a reason not to trust a first run:

- **A block usually has several models.** A stair is `_stairs`, `_stairs_inner` and `_stairs_outer`; a door is four; a fence is a post and a side. The tool tries every variant and takes the best match, because comparing against the first file whose name matches reports nearly everything as wrong.
- **A rotation is not a disagreement.** The comparison is done on the sorted extents, so a model that differs only by which way it faces agrees.
- **A connecting shape has to be dumped unconnected**, or a fence in open air is compared against a crossroads.
- **Some families are named differently on each side** — our *Emberite* is its *netherite*, our *stowbox* its *shulker box*, our *Bramble* its *creeper*, our *void pearl* its *ender pearl*.

> **Three deliberate divergences, named rather than hidden behind a wider tolerance** — because a *different* disagreement on one of them is still a fault worth seeing. Primed **TNT** is lifted one texel and a `static_assert` holds it there; the **redstone torch** paints its head on the stick where the reference adds zero-thickness glow quads round it; and the **bell** includes the bell itself, which the reference draws as a block entity and leaves out of `bell_floor.json` altogether.

> ⛔ **That last one is why the bell was wrong three times.** There is no block model for a bell body anywhere in the reference — `bell_floor.json` is the *frame* only — so the geometry had to come off the artwork instead, and guessing it gave a body that shared a plane with the bar above it and sampled the transparent column beside its own texture as a stripe. It is five boxes now: two stone posts, a plank bar, a six-wide body hanging a hair *into* the bar so the two never share a plane, and the flared lip under it.

### A dropped block is a miniature of the block

`ItemEntities::buildMesh` used to draw every non-flat block item as **one spinning cube** wearing the block's side texture, so a dropped bell was a gold brick, a dropped torch a cube of torch and a dropped fence a plank. It now draws the block's real boxes, scaled into the drop's own half-extent, with a model's own rectangles and layers where it has them.

**A block is drawn in four places and they have to be told the same things.** The mesher, the falling cube, `appendBlockIcon`, and `ItemEntities::buildMesh` are four separate implementations of "draw this block as boxes". **They now share more than the box list: `world/FaceGeometry.hpp` owns the cube-corner table, the winding and the shading, and all four read it.** That table used to be written out in each of them, and every copy had been wrong at least once — the falling cube's shades drifted from the mesher's on five of six faces, its corner rows were the mesher's *reversed* (a V-flip on all 24 corners and an inward winding on all 6 faces, so a falling block was upside-down and inside-out against the block that had been standing there a moment earlier), and the dropped item's four wall rows had their first and last pairs exchanged, mirroring every dropped and thrown block. `ChunkMesher.cpp` is the authority the table was lifted from, unchanged, because its rows are the ones validated against the reference's `models/block/*.json`. **Four copies agreeing today is not four copies agreeing after the next edit**, and the last three of those faults were found by eye, in play, milestones after they were written.

Two more faults of exactly that shape were found by play on 2026-08-11, one in each of the non-mesher paths, and both were invisible from the world:

- **The drop computed one side layer and handed it to all four side quads.** `blockTextureLayer` decides "is this the front" by comparing the direction it is given against the block's facing, so passing `blockFacing(block)` four times says *front* four times — a sticky piston wore its plate right round. Each quad now gets its own `NegZ / PosZ / PosX / NegX`. A piston pointing up looked correct throughout, by luck: `blockFacing` answers `Unknown` for vertical facings and that hits a different branch.
- **The icon painted the side layer on the lid of any model-shaped block**, and ignored a `ModelBox`'s own `lidLayer` and `sideLayer` entirely. An end portal frame lost its eye socket and read as a plain sandy cube. The drop had been doing this correctly all along, so the fix was to make the icon agree with it.

The standing lesson in `CLAUDE.md` is to ask where else a block is drawn whenever you change how one looks. These two say more than that: **the three paths differ in what they are willing to be told.** The mesher always has a real per-face direction, the icon has two side faces needing two directions, and the drop has four. Any of them that quietly settles for one answer is wrong for every block whose faces differ.

**`iconBoxes(BlockId)` is the single owner of which boxes that is**, and the hotbar's slot picture reads the same function — so what is on the floor and what is in your hand cannot disagree. `usesModelIcon(shape)` is the matching question for the shapes built from `postModel` instead.

> **The 2D sprite path is untouched and must stay that way.** `usesFlatIcon` — Cross, Flat, Ladder, Vine, Pane — plus every non-block item still draws as its flat picture given real thickness by `appendSpriteModel`. A flower, a ladder, a pane of glass, a tool, a spawn egg and a bucket are *pictures*, and turning any of them into a little cube is the opposite mistake.

**`drop_showcase=1` throws one of every awkward block on the floor** a few paces north of the spawn point, with the sprite-path drops beside them for comparison. Dropped items are never saved, so it leaves nothing behind.

### Per-block tables are swept at compile time, and the stride is why it fits

**A per-block table that is a plain runtime function in a `.cpp` can carry neither a `static_assert` nor a sweep, and that is how a hundred and twenty blocks sat on the wrong blast resistance through three clean builds and a soak.** The fix each time is the same: make the function `constexpr`, move it to a header, and walk every block id at compile time asserting the invariants the table is supposed to hold.

**Seven files now carry one**, on top of `Block.hpp`'s own `everyBlockNamed` and `everyBlockTextured`:

| Sweep | File | What it walks |
|---|---|---|
| `SoundSweep` | `core/Sounds.hpp` | `soundMaterialFor` — no `Ladder` shape at `Stone`, no planks-parented block at `Stone`, `isGlassBlock ⇒ Glass` |
| `MiningSweep` | `item/Mining.hpp` | hardness, tool, tier, drop gate |
| `DropSweep` | `item/BlockDrops.hpp` | what each block drops and how many |
| `BlastSweep` | `world/Explosion.hpp` | blast resistance |
| `CookSweep` | `world/Furnace.cpp` | cook speed, and that any fuel with a remainder does not stack |
| `DropModelSweep` | `world/ItemEntity.cpp` | the drop's boxes against the mesher's |
| `CopperSweep` | `world/Copper.hpp` | the oxidation and waxing round trips |

**The stride exists because MSVC gives a single constant expression about 100,000 steps.** Walking every block id in one `constexpr` loop blows that budget, so each sweep is written as a function taking a pass number, covering `[pass * stride, pass * stride + stride)`, with one `static_assert` per pass. Six of the seven run **512 ids × 7 passes** (7 × 512 = 3,584, comfortably over `kBlockIdCount` — which was **3,309** at the last probe on 2026-08-19), and a `static_assert` in each file proves the passes cover the range — so adding blocks past 3,584 fails the build rather than silently going unchecked. **`CopperSweep` is 128 × 26 instead**, because its body does far more work per id and the same budget buys fewer ids. If a new sweep will not fit, shorten the stride; do not thin the invariant. ⚠️ **The lower ceiling is still not this one, but it moved today.** `Mining.hpp` splits its table into 256-id chunks, and its `static_assert(kMiningChunkCount <= kMiningChunkCapacity)` fired at **3,328** until 10:23:32 on 2026-08-19 and at **3,584** after — the same number these sweeps reach. Both are now 3,584; if either side moves again, `Mining.hpp` is the one to check first, because its supply of chunks is hand-written while its demand is derived.

**Five blocks were reshaped to `BlockShape::Model` this round** — `Candle`, `Bamboo`, `SeaPickle`, `Lectern` and `DragonEgg` — each moving from an approximating shape to its real boxes, and a `static_assert` in `Block.hpp` names all five so that a shape table edit that quietly demotes one of them fails the build.

## World Persistence

Generation is a pure function of `(seed, chunkCoord)`, so an untouched chunk is already perfectly reproducible. A save is therefore the **difference** between the generated world and the played one, which keeps it small no matter how far the player travels.

A chunk is flagged `modified` the moment `setBlock` changes something, and only flagged chunks are ever written. The write happens **immediately before the chunk is erased** on unload — not queued — because a modified chunk erased before writing would silently revert. Loading checks disk first and falls back to the generator.

Each chunk is one file under `saves/world_<seed>/chunks/`, written to a `.tmp` name and then **renamed**. Rename is atomic on Windows and POSIX, so the file on disk is always either the complete old version or the complete new one, never a mixture.

Every file carries a header with magic, format version, seed, its own coordinates and block count, **all four checked on load**. This is the only place the game reads bytes it did not produce this run, so it validates rather than assumes.

> ⛔ **Chunks and the player file carry separate version constants, and that separation is load-bearing.** `kChunkFormatVersion` (currently **6**) versions chunk files; `kFormatVersion` (currently **4**) versions `player.dat`. **Bumping the chunk version is how a worldgen fix reaches a world that has already been played** — every stale chunk fails its header check and is regenerated. Doing that must not cost the player their inventory or position, which is exactly why the two numbers are not one. Waterlogging bumped the chunk version to 2; the 16-bit block id bumped it to 3; 4 → 5 on 2026-08-17 for the ground-cover fix that ends the bare bands at y 32 and y 64; **5 → 6 on 2026-08-18, for a whole round of generation fixes at once** — cave carving order, multi-block plants no longer truncated at the chunk ceiling, two inversions corrected in the rarest-first ore table, `veinHeight` made the reference's own sum rather than a 50/50 mixture, `kShallowBedDepth` 6 → 1 (a reference y-distance never converted into our 96-block world), a ramped rather than stepped coastline factor, and four fixed interior collisions in village buildings. **There is no migration for this number and there cannot be one**: a record version can be migrated because a record is a list of fields and a field can be remapped, but terrain is not a field, it is the whole chunk. So this version means **discard and regenerate**, the check in `load` is a strict `!=` for that reason, and widening it to also accept 5 "to keep what people built" is a bump that changes nothing — which this project has already paid for once.
>
> **`kFormatVersion` 4 means two things at once, and deliberately shares one number.** The record grew `SavedPlayer::enderChest`, *and* **eighteen duplicate item ids were deleted** from the catalogue — fifteen music discs carrying Mojang's own track titles that sat above the saddle for five milestones with no reader, plus three brewing reagents that were Mojang-named copies of already-renamed ids — sliding every id above them down. Both landed on 2026-08-18 and both need a version 3 file read differently, so they take one version and **one migration** rather than each claiming a 4 and quietly disagreeing about what a 4 contains. Nothing older is refused: a version 2 and a version 3 file are each a stated prefix-free struct (`LegacyPlayerV2`, `LegacyPlayerV3`) copied across **field by field** — `damage` included, because a stowbox's handle rides in it and an upgrade that reset it would empty every stowbox in the world.
>
> **The three block entities and the creature table carry their own.** `kFurnaceVersion` is at **4**, `kChestVersion` at **3** and `kStowboxVersion` at **2**, all bumped by the same item-id renumbering; `kCreatureVersion` is at **5**, having gained the `PopulatedColumn` table so that which chunks have already had their one-off herd survives a restart. **Version 4 of the creature file is rejected rather than migrated even though it looks readable**, because it was never frozen and shipped — it moved at least once inside this tree without a bump, which is precisely why it cannot be trusted to have moved only once. The cost is one herd on a developer's machine; the alternative is reading a record whose meaning is unknown. The M29m edit that produced 4 also widened `kind` to `std::int32_t` and gave the tail a named `reserved` byte: as a `std::uint8_t` it left a three-byte hole, and the padding meant **four uninitialised bytes per creature were written to disk on every save**.
>
> **Version 2 was migrated rather than discarded for a while, and that upgrade path has now been retired.** Widening each id in place was lossless and saved a player's building, which was the right call at the time — and it also meant that anything wrong in a version-2 chunk could never be reached by any later fix. M24 found exactly that: a sheet of water hanging in mid-air, left by a long-deleted test harness, in a chunk two versions old. Bumping the current version did nothing, because the bad file was not the current version. **A migration path is a promise that old data stays; check what that promise costs before making it, and be willing to withdraw it.**
>
> **An out-of-date version is now rejected silently**, unlike a wrong magic number, seed or coordinate. It is not a fault — it is this number doing the job it exists for, and warning about it would print one line per chunk in the world. See `CLAUDE.md` on warning about faults rather than about states the user chose.
>
> This matters more often than it sounds. Water flow calls `setBlock`, which flags a chunk modified, so **merely standing near an ocean writes chunks to disk**. A generator fix that tests clean can still be plainly broken on screen because the world being loaded predates it.

Player position and view direction live in `player.dat` beside the chunks, furnace contents in `furnaces.dat`, chest contents in `chests.dat`, the contents of stowboxes that are currently *items* in `stowboxes.dat`, and the creature population in `creatures.dat`. All five side tables follow the same shape: magic, version, seed, count, then fixed-size records written as raw bytes and `static_assert`ed trivially copyable. An empty table deletes its file rather than leaving a stale one — a leftover would restore furnaces the player has broken, or repopulate a world they have cleared.

> ⭐ **Village loot needed none of this, and that is the point of the `LootChest` marker.** An unrolled chest is a block id, so it costs nothing but the chunk it already lives in; a rolled one is a plain chest in `chests.dat` like any other. The conversion is a `setBlock`, which flags the chunk modified, so the chunk is loaded rather than regenerated from then on and the roll cannot repeat. **`saveChests` discards an empty chest rather than writing it**, which is exactly why the marker had to be consumed at roll time: *open → empty → save → reload* would otherwise have found the marker still in place and re-rolled it. No format bump, no new file, no new record — see "Chest loot".

`player.dat` also carries health, food, saturation and exhaustion since M21, and **everything the player is carrying since M29m** — all thirty-six slots, hotbar first, plus which hotbar slot is in hand. **A version-1 file is not migrated, it is refused**, which costs nothing: the player reappears at the default spawn with a full bar rather than at whatever four zeroes would mean, which is dead.

> ⛔ **The inventory was not saved anywhere at all until M29m.** `player.dat` was 48 bytes of position and vitals, so every launch handed back an empty inventory — in survival, that is the whole game. It is now 484: twelve of header, thirty-six of vitals, thirty-six slots at twelve bytes each and the selected slot.
>
> **Version 2 is read rather than refused**, through a `LegacyPlayerV2` record that states its own seven fields and is copied across by name. A prefix read would have been shorter and is exactly the silent layout promise this file's rule about "a stated list of fields" exists to stop. Refusing instead would have cost every existing world its position and health for nothing, since a version 2 file has no inventory to lose.
>
> **What comes back is checked, not trusted.** An item id outside the run would index the name and sprite tables off the end, so an unknown slot is dropped, every count is clamped to what that item may stack to, and the selected slot is clamped to the hotbar. Same rule as the health clamp beside it: this is the one place the game reads bytes it did not write this run.
>
> A saved inventory **replaces** the creative starting kit rather than merging with it, so a slot deliberately emptied stays empty — but only when the save actually carried something, or a version 2 world would arrive and wipe the kit on the strength of an inventory that was never written.

### When a save happens

**Three triggers, and the third is the one that exists for the crash.** A **~30 s timer** in the frame loop, a **flag set when a screen closes** on a container whose contents may have changed, and `SaveOnUnwind` — a destructor declared beside `world` so it runs *while the world is still alive*.

> ⛔ **The emergency save cannot live in `main`'s `catch`, and that is the whole reason the destructor exists.** Unwinding destroys the block's locals — `world`, the player, every container — **before** an enclosing handler runs, so a save written there reads freed memory. A destructor declared alongside them runs first, because destruction is the reverse of construction. It swallows its own exceptions and says so in the log, since a throw out of a destructor during unwinding calls `std::terminate` and would replace the real reason the game died.

> ⛔ **Everything except terrain was written exactly once, after the frame loop, until 2026-08-17** — inside a `try` whose `catch` did not save. A lost device or a pulled cable therefore cost the whole session's inventory, chests, furnaces and creatures **while keeping the terrain they stood in**, which is the worst of both: a world that looks played and is empty.

**The autosave and the screen give-back read the same list of "stacks that exist only while a screen is up".** `forEachScreenStack` names the cursor stack and the crafting grid, and skips a furnace's two slots because those are a view onto a block that saves itself. It is one function because two callers need the answer, and the first autosave written had only one of them — a world reloaded with the cursor stack and the crafting grid gone. Saving walks an **inventory copy** with those stacks added, never a live give-back: `rewindDrag` reassigns `heldStack` every frame, so a real give-back at save time double-adds.

> ⚠️ **Known gap: items lying on the ground are still not saved.** `WorldStore` has no drops table, so a save is silent about them and everything on the floor is gone on reload. Pre-existing, not introduced by the autosave, and it is the reason drops can be described as wall-timed rather than tick-timed in "Items and drops". Closing it is a new file on the same magic-version-seed pattern the other five use.

One file per chunk is deliberately crude: a bad write damages exactly one chunk and it needs no index to stay consistent. A packed region format belongs with M13 if file count ever becomes the problem.
